An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Furthermore, a comparison with previous findings from D0 and CDF II revealed a more precise measurement, and also a first estimate of the $C\Gamma_{B^0_s}$ parameter which equals 0.059 ± 0.014. Additionally, this research included constraints on rare $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay rates to decay rates of other rare processes, such as $B^0_s\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0\rightarrow K^+K^-$, with rates less than 4.4 × 10^-7, 5.4 × 10^-7, and 2.6 × 10^-7 respectively. Lastly, it was observed that the $B^0_s$ vacuum instability period is likely extended to 2011 or later.

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. Lastly, we have made our raw data available to the public in the form of tables that can be used for further analysis and validation of models. The techniques and results presented in this study also offer valuable opportunities for exploring new variables and expanding the existing knowledge of particle flow in collisions. The underlying data can be accessed at this link: https://doi.org/10.17182/hepgdc.hepdata.productions.831645.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Lastly, we offer a concise overview of our framework and its potential applications in database settings, along with two examples that demonstrate the practical utility of our framework. Moreover, we outline future research possibilities and explore connections between our work and established theories, including fuzzy logic, semantic data integration, and database repair. Lastly, we make our research implementation available for public use.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed framework is termed DeepHMap++ and its code has been made publicly available.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. All in all, this research highlights a set of numerical methods that biologically relevant simulations can leverage to enhance accuracy while maintaining speed.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. A comprehensive discussion of existing and newly observed phenomena in the surface-seal regime is also presented. Moreover, our research includes an analytical model of the water-entry Pinch-off Time, valid for the first time across all impact velocity ranges. Furthermore, our analysis of the formed cavity's pressure patterns and water-entry stages has been incorporated into our work, alongside an in-depth examination of our results. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. The theoretical predictions discussed in this paper have been validated through accurate experimental measurements of both dark exciton populations as well as the emitted phonon bundles. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. We also explore the durability of these states in noisy environments, discovering that they resist degradation more effectively than certain other non-classical states. Ultimately, our research highlights the immense utility of SPCCSs, as they are exceptionally resilient and exhibit a wide range of non-classical properties, making them exceptionally precious for various quantum applications. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. By addressing these challenges, we can improve the accessibility and utility of NLP tools for significant populations using code-mixed language.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. I discuss feasible routes to evaluating systems using smaller, more manageable description sets, including selecting existing data more thoughtfully, generating additional data, or creating simple evaluation tasks that complement description quality assessments. These approaches prioritize practicality and accuracy in system evaluation. I also examine feasible methods for assessing system accuracy using qualitative metrics, such as category analysis and counterfactual reasoning. These methods prioritize the practicality of evaluation processes. Ultimately, I believe we require more diverse description datasets that account for various visual elements and situations. I propose several possible research directions for evaluating image description systems systematically. These directions involve analyzing existing datasets, developing novel evaluation methods, integrating description quality with other systems, and creating realistic simulation environments that mimic real-world situations. These environments could be used to evaluate and train systems on various tasks, including those involving multiple images and interactive scenarios. I also discuss the connection between description quality and system usability for visually impaired users. I propose simple, effective evaluation methods, including evaluating systems based on their accuracy in describing specific categories of images, generating detailed descriptions of individual images, and creating interactive descriptions of multiple images. I believe we should prioritize system usability through description quality, along with other methods, such as providing detailed documentation and conducting regular accessibility tests. I demonstrate the feasibility of these evaluation methods by training a system to describe categories of images and evaluating its performance on a small, carefully selected description dataset. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. Ultimately, this research has clarified the crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$, and provides a method for predicting its electronic behavior in other situations.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In contrast to purely digital explanations, our study highlighted the significant role of The Big Sort in the circulation of misinformation, demonstrating that solutions to this issue require an interdisciplinary approach that takes into account both online and offline factors. We also provided a code for researching Reddit comments at https://github.com/colbertj/reddit_geosort.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. The results presented in this study contribute a unique analysis of human speech during robotic teaching and provide an invaluable dataset for future robotic learning research. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. This paper also introduces a basic prototype of an automated testing framework called CTF, and presents empirical evidence of the efficacy of this prototype. This evidence is derived from various systematic assessments of CTF, including a case study involving a real-world system. This study has implications for the ongoing debate surrounding specification-based validation methods for conversational systems. This research has further potential in identifying approaches to develop robust and efficient learning algorithms for deep learning-based conversational agents, particularly those employing memory-based models. This paper also makes available the complete code for CTF, an open-source testing framework for conversational agents, at the following location: https://github.com/amaniya/ctf. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The proposed approach also achieves meaningful interpretability results, enabling the incorporation of domain-specific importance weights to further enhance performance. The code for MSDCR is publicly available at https://github.com/zhoukai1997/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The proposed method can be applied to a wide range of optimization applications, including multistage robust optimization, dynamic fully convex two-stage robust optimization, and stochastic linear programming. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. This research was conducted in collaboration with the NeuroIMCU project, an initiative aimed at standardizing MRI data analysis and quality control, and has been incorporated into the MRIQC pipeline as a default approach. NeuroIMCU promotes consistent data preprocessing and quality control through uniform analysis protocols and comprehensive, reproducible code. This has been achieved by detailing the neuroimaging analysis pipeline Neuro, alongside the results of this study, which are available on NeuroIMCU's Neuroverse platform at https://neuroimcu.github.io/results/mriqc-generalization/. To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks. Ultimately, a robust model has been presented that accounts for complex relationships between transportation modes, EV charging, and grid recovery. A notable finding from this model is that owning a private EV can actually decrease system resilience in some cases, counter to common perceptions, by increasing the spread of transportation-related congestion that hinders grid recovery. To limit the spread of congestion and maximize resilience, it has been shown that limiting EV charging to specific hours or reducing grid recovery speeds can be effective, as these measures help prevent widespread congestion that hinders grid recovery. On the other hand, increasing the speed of grid recovery or offering incentives for non-resilient transportation choices, it has been demonstrated, can also decrease resilience, highlighting the balance that must be struck between these opposing forces. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Consequently, this research extends the Motivation Dynamics family to include a prominent example involving multiple agents, a control system configuration that ensures safe and successful meetings, and a performance metric that validates successful completion of targeted tasks. Moreover, it highlights the potential applications and limitations of this complex pattern in a real-world setting, where two agents repeatedly meet at designated locations in a dynamic environment. The code for this research is available online at https://github.com/NeuroRendezvous/MRD2. The research was funded by the Office of Naval Research, with specific grant numbers provided in the acknowledgments section. The findings were also presented during the 2022 American Control Conference.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, we explored the phase stability and energy of different structures for these materials, finding that AuCu3 is the most stable phase, followed by a Ni2In structure, and then a Mo2C structure. Lastly, our findings suggest that the AuCu3 structure can be obtained from the Ni2In structure via a phase transition induced by lattice distortion. Additionally, we identified possible lattice vibrations that could indicate a relationship between the electronic and lattice properties of these materials. Lastly, our study classified the electronic bands of the AuCu3 structure and highlighted the role of Cm 5d and Sn 5p orbital hybridization in the magnetic moment reduction observed in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. Predicted particles include 13 possible baryons and 55 possible mesons, with masses ranging from a few GeV to over 100 GeV, and properties that could be determined with a 100 GeV beam of protons. The bilepton model also predicts that certain processes will occur at higher rates than predicted by the standard model, such as the decay of a proton into neutral mesons or the creation of heavy baryons and mesons during particle collisions. The authors propose searching for these predictions at the Fermilab Tevatron, the Large Hadron Collider, or future particle accelerators like the Future Circular Collider. The bilepton model can be verified or disproved by detecting the predicted particles or examining high-energy collision data for evidence of rare processes that break the standard model. The model's predictive power makes it a promising area of study for particle physics beyond the standard model. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Both of these results generalize existing knowledge from Sn to the group Bn. Additionally, our work offers a solution to a problem posed by E.M. Levi, which involves calculating the number of ordered generating sequences for the group Bn. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Greater precision can be achieved with higher spatial resolution galaxy surveys and better photometric data, such as those from the James Webb Space Telescope, its successors, and similar missions. Ultimately, this research highlights a previously underutilized source of information about the large-scale structure of the universe, namely the lens-induced scattering of SN Ia magnitudes, which can be used in conjunction with other cosmological probes in the current generation of dark matter and dark energy surveys. Given its narrow dependence on the properties of dark matter and dark energy, this analysis paves the way for a complementary signal of the universe's structure and its evolution that can be accurately modeled and matched to observational data, in accordance with the principles of Bayesian statistics. Given its broad applicability to SN Ia data from various datasets, we demonstrate this approach using the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and predict a similar outcome with the PES and SNe Ia datasets. Given its potential for further development, this analysis paves the way for combining the effects of lensing and the intrinsic scatter of SN Ia on the estimation of cosmological parameters, which can be achieved with better data and better galaxy mass calibration, in accordance with the principles of Bayesian statistics. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. To further enhance research momentum, we are making available high-resolution images of T center distributions across multiple bulk samples and device layers. These findings are expected to facilitate large-scale production and exploration of this promising quantum technology.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality for a small positive value $\varepsilon$ and variational methods, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for a multiplicity of the system's solutions given the given conditions. Additionally, as an alternative, we can also show the system's solutions' regularity. The approach also involves obtaining a result for a system of equations that contains the singular Trudinger-Moser inequality as a key element in a variational approach. The main paper consists of five sections. The introduction to the system, the Trudinger-Moser inequality, and some essential notation can be found in the first section. The second section is devoted to the system's weak solutions and its regularity. The third section is dedicated to establishing the singular Trudinger-Moser inequality as a key element in a variational approach. The fourth section is where we can find the system's multiple solution possibilities. The fifth and final section is where we can find the system's regularity. The main paper also includes two appendices. The first appendix is a version of the Trudinger-Moser inequality for a domain in $\mathbb{R}^2$. The second appendix is devoted to the definition of a function that belongs to the space $H^1_0(\Omega)$'s dual, and some of its key elements. We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. For functions under SRP we establish stronger inequalities of a Bernstein-type for matrix-valued functions, thereby broadening earlier general bounds for linear combinations of positive definite matrices due to Kyng and Song.

Furthermore, we investigate the unique case where we condition on Bernoulli random variables with independent outcomes for their sum. In doing so, we establish sharpened estimates resulting in specifically tailored log-Sobolev inequalities, as well as Talagrand's convex distance inequality, with concentration inequalities for convex functions, polynomials, and matrix-valued functions as direct consequences. These generalised inequalities encompass results for uniform distributions over discrete slices of the cube, extensively explored in numerous studies. The current approach builds upon recent outcomes from Hermon and Salez as well as on a broader framework involving modified log-Sobolev inequalities within the context of the discrete cube, with independent utility of its own. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Unlike the case with the general linear group, however, these characteristics cannot be arranged in a linear pattern. Instead, they form a group isomorphic to the Weyl group of type B_n, and only the conjugacy classes associated with odd-n scenarios incorporate an extra layer of distinction, defined by the sign of the determinant. Furthermore, Springer established that each conjugacy class can be reached through a symplectic transformation with a specific structure, described as a sequence of operations that alternates between adding a multiple of the identity and swapping two basis elements in a manner consistent with the rules governing Hermitian forms. This process is essentially equivalent to the procedure used to calculate the orbit of a point under the action of a Coxeter group. In the process of analyzing these conjugacy classes, Springer also discovered several patterns related to the number of irreducible components within a system of Hermitian forms, as well as the associated polynomial degrees. In the specific case of Sp_4(K), he demonstrated that the conjugacy classes can be categorized based on the number of components in the system of Hermitian forms, and that each class is uniquely defined by these criteria. In contrast, the case of Sp_n(K) for n greater than four does not exhibit a similar pattern, with conjugacy classes depending on the specific system of Hermitian forms rather than the number of components. Finally, Springer also investigated the relationship between the conjugacy classes of Sp_n(K) and the symmetric powers of the finite field K, obtaining results that generalize the principles applied in the specific case of Sp_4(K). These generalizations involve considering Shoda pairs within the symmetric power of degree n+2, and demonstrating that they define conjugacy classes within the symplectic group of the same n dimension. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. We also explore various scenarios to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the issue. By developing a general framework, our research can be applied to other transplant organ situations, such as lungs, liver, and intestines, which also face incompatibility problems. The economic and societal benefits of this research are significant, given the critical need for kidney donors. The optimal acceptance criteria can be a valuable tool for allocating kidneys within the current system, and even more so in emerging biotechnology areas, such as xenotransplantation, where the level of incompatibility may be substantially reduced. The approach presented in this paper offers a promising solution to the challenge of incompatibility, which could be a major hurdle in these developments. The economic costs of treating graft failure are a crucial consideration, which is a direct result of accepting incompatible kidneys. Therefore, it is necessary to model this cost within the decision-making process. The proposed model incorporates this critical information, and provides a more accurate representation of the situation. The model also accounts for different levels of incompatibility, which can be measured by matching grades, such as the degree of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) mismatch. The model assumes that this level of incompatibility remains constant over time, which may not always be the case, and can change due to various factors, such as the progression of disease. To address this issue, a more complex model is introduced that takes into account the dynamic change in incompatibility. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work offers a mathematical framework that can be extended to unveil the underlying structures of various NLP embeddings, providing a precise theoretical understanding of how these models generate embeddings and offering a means of evaluating the quality of these embeddings. We also discuss various learning regret-based benchmarks that financial researchers can use to validate the quality of word2vec embeddings in specific contexts. Our research suggests that the cosine similarity alone is an inadequate metric for evaluating the performance of these models, given their propensity to confuse antonyms as frequentist synonyms. Our analysis of financial corpora reveals the importance of considering time-varying patterns in word2vec embeddings, offering implications for financial applications such as firm clustering, sentiment analysis, and risk analysis. Our results further highlight the challenges of disentangling the mixed distribution of word2vec embeddings, posing questions for the research community and potential areas of innovation in NLP. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/abhinavk91/w2f_nyc.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. 
A hybrid fast time-diviation multiple access (FTD-MTA) scheme is proposed to implement the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values in practice.
In a simulated scenario, we show that the proposed SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems outperform the conventional baseband OFDM systems. 
A prototype based on the SISO-OFDM system is implemented to demonstrate the feasibility of the ideal waveforming strategy. 
A non-optimal, yet simple, zero-padding (ZP)-OFDM based FTD-MTA scheme is proposed as a practical solution. 
By simulating a real-world scenario, we show that the ZP-OFDM based FTD-MTA system provides nearly the same performance as the ideal waveforming strategy. 
In a real-time experiment, we successfully transmitted both data and energy to a far-field receiver, using the ZP-OFDM based FTD-MTA system. 
In the experiment, we found that the ZP-OFDM based FTD-MTA system is robust to various environment scenarios. 
We conclude that the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems are practical solutions for IDET systems. 
For the MISO-OFDM system, we investigate the impact of different antenna configurations and carrier configurations on the system's performance. 
We recommend a specific antenna and carrier configuration as the optimal solution. 
In the paper, we also investigate the possibility of implementing the ZP-OFDM based FTD-MTA system in a near-field setting.

We derive the theoretical expression of the TFD-MTA system's performance, which provides valuable insights into the ideal waveforming strategy.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Furthermore, we have achieved consistent results compared to other level-set methods, with significant improvements in implementing numerical operations on the fluid--solid interface. The development of our approach has been fully integrated into the existing OpenFOC software, with notable enhancements to its level-set capabilities. The code has been extensively tested to demonstrate the validity and performance of this hybrid method. The current implementation has been optimized for scalar models and includes a detailed evaluation of the method's performance against a range of problems, from simple Stefan problems to more complex scenarios like melting cells and solidifying films. The code is now available as a separate branch within the OpenFOC project on GitHub. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This study is further distinguished by the incorporation of a rationalization-related performance gap term in the sample complexity lower bound, a novel aspect in multiagent learning setting settings. Our results also extend to settings with finite action spaces and model knowledge, as well as to the specific case of learning a CCE. The developed algorithms have been evaluated through numerical experiments, showcasing their performance in realistic scenarios. This study's findings also belong to the broader category of results known as "positive result about the effect of a large number of agents on learning in games". This work is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.02463. The code for the results presented in this paper is available at https://github.com/learning-in-games/rationalizable-equilibria. The numerical experiments described in this paper were conducted using Learning in Games Toolbox, a MATLAB package available at https://github.com/learning-in-games/LGT. The results of this paper were previously published in a conference titled Proceedings of the 39th International Conference on Machine Learning, a conference associated with a clear connection to the field of artificial intelligence. An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread. This model is equivalent to a specific version of the classic birth-death process, where it results in a discrete distribution instead of a continuous distribution. This version of the model is unique as it allows for the possibility of complete eradication of the infections. This model is also relevant to understanding phenomena such as the spread of diseases among animal populations, where immunity does not last forever, and individuals can become infected again. This model can also be used to describe the spread of diseases among populations that move freely between different groups, where the discipline of not mixing with infected individuals is not 100% faithful. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. By tailoring the importance of historical data, the variance reduction based experience replay framework uncovers a multitude of modification possibilities, presenting a versatile framework for the reinforcement learning community. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. The code is available for download at [www.mgglam.com].

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We show that in the limit where multiple SLE is driven by these models with a parameter tending to infinity, the associated Gaussian free fields converge to the harmonic measure in the upper half-plane and the fields associated with the slits in the first orthant of the complex plane. Additionally, we provide an alternative interpretation of the results established by Sheffield and Choudary, Miller, and Sheffield. Lastly, we provide a description of the fields associated with the multiple SLE on the Riemann surface obtained by gluing two domains mentioned earlier along their associated marked points. This description enables us to extend the concept of an imaginary surface to this more general setting. Furthermore, we establish that in the limit where multiple SLE is driven by the Dyson model or the Bru-Wishart process with a parameter tending to infinity, the associated Gaussian free field converges to the harmonic measure in the combined domain. Lastly, we provide a solution to a stochastic version of a problem initially asked by C. Hong, which involves the asymptotic analysis of a specific arrangement of random rays in the complex plane. This solution enables us to extend the concept of an imaginary surface to the complex plane by means of these rays, resulting in a Gaussian free field associated with multiple SLE on a Riemann surface obtained by gluing two copies of the complex plane along two marked points, with the field converging to the harmonic measure in the combined domain in the limit where multiple SLE is driven by the Dyson model or the Bru-Wishart process with a parameter tending to infinity. Since the ultralight dark matter can be adequately modeled as a classical field, this interaction's effect is reflected in a periodic oscillation in the number of decay events. Nevertheless, we find that in the early universe, this interaction would almost certainly disrupt standard cosmological outcomes. Moreover, the condition that neutrinos had to have begun freely moving by the point of matter-radiation equality significantly limits the permissible parameter space, meaning even future $0 \nu \beta \beta$ decay experiments with a meV sensitivity to the effective neutrino mass would have difficulty detecting a signal. Despite this, we notice that in the instance where neutrinoless double beta decay is observed, it could be necessary to re-examine the standard cosmological outcomes, albeit requiring very small neutrino masses. Furthermore, detecting a cosmological influence directly, either through the large scale structure or the cosmic microwave background, could also be necessary for a complete understanding of this phenomenon. The interplay between neutrino and dark matter, facilitated by the extremely light dark matter field interacting with neutrinos, could be assessed through a variety of theoretical frameworks, with the consequence of neutrinoless double beta decay driven by this interaction being independent of these frameworks. The relation between the decay rate and the neutrino and dark matter masses is extremely straightforward, allowing future experimental or observational inputs to be straightforwardly incorporated, with the outcome being a direct proportionality between the decay rate and the square of the average dark matter density in the location of the experiment, modified by the neutrino mass squared. The accessibility of this interaction to direct detection is highly unlikely, with even the most sensitive experiments being incapable of detecting it, due to the extremely light nature of the dark matter. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. Moreover, this method was integrated into a renowned conversational agent evaluation metric and discovered a 25% increase in Semantic Variety. The code for this research has been made publically accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ParthGhosh/Diversity_in_Dialogue.

Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. In the second scenario, the simulation stopped at the point the star reached its maximum possible size due to gravitational pressure, rather than breaking down to a white dwarf. This could provide a possible endpoint for low-mass star formation, often overlooked in scientific text. This could provide a foundation for further study on the endpoints of sub-stellar objects, brown dwarfs, and other low-mass stars. A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components. By utilizing this novel model, comprehensive calculations have been performed for various afterglow phenomena, including the distribution of radiated energy, luminosity, and synthesized elements. These calculations have been applied to various astrophysical scenarios, such as supernovae, massive star explosions, compact object mergers, and collapsing neutron stars, and have been compared with empirical observations, including gamma-ray bursts, X-ray and optical spectra, and synthesized elements. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. Although this design has been previously proposed, our analysis highlights a more efficient implementation using state-of-the-art materials and emphasizes the significance of optimizing component parameters in optimizing the detector's performance. Our findings suggest that with current technology, the sloshing Sagnac interferometer configuration could achieve optimal overall detector performance, achieving ten times the sensitivity of the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup above $10\,Hz$ or better snr for specific neutron star merger waveforms. Consequently, this design has the potential to enhance the detection capabilities of future gravitational wave detectors equipped with neutron star merger templates. Moreover, this design possesses robustness against misalignment, which facilitates efficient operation. Lastly, this detector configuration offers feasible opportunities for combining quantum entanglement with gravitational wave detection, providing insights that could lead to novel ideas for future detectors. Our research is compatible with ongoing projects such as Eco and AdvLIGO+, demonstrating that upgrading these detectors to the described design would result in better detections and greater scientific return. Ultimately, the entwined nature of optical and quantum loss presents a unified challenge for future gravitational wave detectors, which can be overcome by implementing a unified analysis based on combined loss parameters, providing a straightforward and universally applicable path to enhancing the performance of a wide range of detectors. Lastly, this paper is accompanied by publicly available software implementing the analysis, available for detecting the effect of loss on detectors and suggests possibilities for improving detectors by changing component parameters, and provides a theoretical explanation for the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, which can be used for teaching purposes.

A question remains regarding the secondary component of GW190814 - whether it's a neutron star or a black hole of minimal mass. Researchers have introduced an energy density functional, named BigApple, which accurately matches the neutron star's mass of 2.60 solar masses and is in line with GW190814's data. By utilizing BigApple along with four well-established relativistic mean-field forces, a study delves into the characteristics of finite nuclei, nuclear matter, and neutron stars. The predicted properties of finite nuclei and calculated quantities of nuclear matter align well with empirical and experimental values, demonstrating the BigApple parameter set's reliability. Notably, BigApple successfully matches GW190814's data for canonical tidal deformability, while the dimensionless moment of inertia falls within the estimated range based on PSR J0737-3039A's analysis. Furthermore, BigApple predicts a characteristic oscillation mode frequency in neutron stars, consistent with predictions derived from PSR J0346+0241's mass and radius estimation. Overall, the BigApple parameter set proves a viable option for studying neutron star properties, finite nuclei, and astrophysical objects.

Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ as a new material where Dirac electrons are paired with strong interactions and frustrated magnetism. Calculations indicate its crystallographic and electronic properties harbor symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level, allowing for multifaceted physics encompassing possible instabilities of charge, magnetism, or superconductivity. By merging various methods to assess its many-body behavior, researchers have observed potential transitions to Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge ordering states, along with $f$-wave unconventional superconductivity in this unique compound. Despite its complexity, researchers believe GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ can be synthesized, and its study holds significant potential for advancing understanding of interplay between different interactions in solid state physics. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Moreover, it highlights the risk of storage units contributing to market instability rather than reducing it. This study also highlights the difference in storage units' response to risk in forward and spot markets, providing further insights into their behavior. Although derived from the Australian market, these findings are expected to be applicable to other regions with similar electricity market characteristics. Therefore, a new model is proposed to incorporate storage units' risk preferences into energy management frameworks, offering a way to address this issue through targeted policy interventions. This model can be applied to other energy storage technologies and other sectors that may also benefit from similar analysis. The research was conducted using computational simulations, and the data used is available for public access. A comment-worthy aspect is that the risk-averse storage units' behavior stands to benefit from innovative risk management products and services, such as range contracts and option contracts, that are now available in the Australian market. This has prompted an examination of these products' structures and the benefits they could provide to the grid, ending with an argument for extending them to other sectors that may also benefit from similar analysis. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. This model highlights the importance of magnetic field-induced coupling between this reservoir and the free Dirac electrons. It also highlights the impact of this coupling on the quantized resistance in the samples. This research reveals the intricate, complex nature of transport properties in HgTe quantum wells, and the necessity of considering their interrelation with the energy spectrum of these structures. This is particularly true when examining the rather rarefied state found in the most slender quantum well constructions. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Additionally, we found that in areas with low mobility, better communication in scheduling modes can come at the expense of longer communication setup times, and that implementing our solution on a semi-static schedule scheduling frame still yields notable benefits. Moreover, in a comparison with a recent static TDD optimization approach, our method delivers higher throughput in a variety of scenarios. Finally, we investigated multiple small cell and mobile scenario cases, finding our solution's scalability and adaptability. Lastly, we proposed a more intricate scheduling strategy, along with simulations confirming its solution's effectiveness. Lastly, we concluded by outlining possible future adaptations and expansions of the game-theoretic solution.

In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations in the model being optimized, as well as consistently outperforming traditional optimization techniques for the artificial task and delivering results on par with standard optimization for MNIST. Nonetheless, more complex HNN models fail to match the baseline for MNIST. Our framework also yields theoretical insights, as we determine that its performance is directly tied to the accuracy with which its latent state mirrors the optimizer's internal state. Our work is accompanied by a simple Hamiltonian Neural Network-based solver for systems with time-dependent coefficients, as well as a derivative model that employs a hybrid approach to tackle problems with difficult initial conditions. Our code is currently available online at the specified URL.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. This approach can be applied to any machine learning model, and we demonstrate its effectiveness using models developed for a specific application. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links.
