The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This finding was further confirmed by analyzing data sets totaling 15 inverse nanobarns of luminosity at two different energy settings, an 8.16 TeV and a 5.02 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. The measured cross-sectional values for both energies aligned with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics, and the ratio of wide-angle hadron production to electron/muon tags was approximately 1.7, as expected from theoretical models of nuclear effects and quantum chromodynamics. The observed top quark production marked the third instance of high-hardness process detection in proton-lead collisions following streamer pixel activation and rare charmed meson decay. The measured cross-sectional values have been made publicly available for use in validating theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. The achieved sensitivity with this analysis protocol lasted approximately 37 seconds in proton-lead collisions at the 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy, and this research paved the way for detecting top quark pairs in lead-lead collisions. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. Moreover, our proposed framework shows promising performance when database contents are accessible, with results showing potential for enhancing existing state-of-the-art models. All proposed approaches are evaluated and demonstrated through additional experiments on the Spider dataset. All code and model weights are available for public access.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. In one representative example, reducing the number of CV folds led to a 8 times decrease in performance estimation variance, thereby successfully addressing the issue of induced bias, and also resulted in a 25% improvement in the overall model performance. In another instance, it led to a 3 times decrease in variance and further enabled the discovery of a linear relationship between optimal epsilon and the standard deviation of the data distribution. In general, our research uncovered a negative exponential correlation between the optimal value of a single parameter (such as epsilon for the SVM) and the standard deviation of the data distribution, as well as a linear connection between another parameter (such as the number of hidden layers for DNNs) and the same metric, which provides a valuable insight into the challenging nature of NLP tasks. In conclusion, our study proposes a straightforward yet effective strategy for reducing the variance of model performance estimates, as well as the uncertainty of the chosen parameters, which amounts to a 100 times decrease in variance in one extreme case, and further enables both efficient and effective tuning of various NLP models. In this regard, our research offers a straightforward and a broad general answer to the question of how to reduce the variance of the objective function with respect to the specified task, which is applicable to any machine learning model and data set. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. Our new model also provides a ready-made implementation for a variety of tasks, such as inference, optimisation and learning, without the need for additional modifications. Our code is now available at https://github.com/alessio-figali/FABE. Our work is further accompanied by a published paper in the proceedings of the IJCAI 2016 conference. We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. Furthermore, we provided specific recommendations for minimizing photon recoil effects in experimental setups. Overall, our study highlighted the significance of considering momentum transfers caused by the interaction between light and matter, and has direct applications for experimenting with precise absorption and emission processes. Ultimately, our findings were validated through direct comparison with theoretical predictions, facilitated by the development of an open-source Monte Carlo code that simulated the absorption process and accounted for the random fluctuations in the absorption pattern resulting from local changes in density within the cloud of ultracold atoms. This simulation tool can be adapted for other similar experiments involving the interaction of light with matter and atomic or molecular gases. Given the general nature of this simulation, it can be applied across a broad spectrum of phenomena, from the absorption of light by gases to the interaction of lasers with semiconductors, and includes features such as interactive graphical visualization of simulation results, as well as the integration of user-defined functions that can be used to describe the behavior of complex systems. It also incorporates features like Monte Carlo simulations, Reynolds transport theorem, and the method of characteristics, and can be utilized through both command line and graphical user interface inputs. The tool has been made available online for public use. An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information. This study's results also contribute to the limited body of research exploring Web search personalisation's effect on the Web. This study's results show that the potential biases in search algorithms are not limited to individual users, but also have ramifications for group performance, indicating that the notion of Web search personalisation being negligible is incorrect. This study's results also demonstrate that the percentage of missed information can be as high as 20%, which is a measurable quantity that has never been previously reported. This study was conducted in New Zealand, so more research is needed to determine if these results are generalisable to other countries. This study's results suggest that the percentage of missed information could be influenced by various elements, including the frequency of Web search, search engine preferences and knowledge of search algorithms' potential biases. Therefore, more research is needed to validate these findings by examining Web search personalisation's effect on knowledge work in different settings, cultures and countries. This research provides a foundation for such future studies by presenting a questionnaire that assesses search algorithms' potential biases, offering actionable data that can be used by researchers and practitioners. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. This has been proven through comparisons of sampling methods, in silico and in human subjects, with a proposed compressed sensing technique of 4D MRI reconstruction. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Furthermore, our method demonstrates this exact algorithm is accurate and reliable, with a difference of just 1% or less when comparing the exact to Monte Carlo results. This exact algorithm can be applied to a variety of contexts, including evaluating the significance of differences in automated summarization, topic modeling, and natural language generation. In addition to paired-permutation testing, our method provides a foundation for developing exact inference techniques in general. This is demonstrated by our derivation of an exact algorithm for paired-friedman testing. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Additionally, this triangulation's flag complex is obtained by applying a graph-theoretical operation called the clique-sum to the 1-skeleton of the loom space's subdivision. A significant outcome of this investigation is the discovery that the triangulation's realization can be determined from the loom space's topology, by examining the loom's local structure near each edge. Furthermore, this realization aligns with the definition of a veering triangulation, which is now recharacterized as a piecewise linear surface with specific properties, generated through a process called regular subdivision, starting from a particular loom space called the reference loom. This new characterization of veering triangulations simplifies their structure, revealing a distilled essence that underlies its complex definition. Moreover, this framework enables the discovery of a key graph theorem, which can be applied to prove outcomes related to the entropy of veering triangulations, originally proven by Agol, Gu\'eritaud, Le, and Shustin, by using a different and more general proof. Lastly, this research introduces an accurate Veering Triangulation Prediction Theorem, which predicts the structure of a veering triangulation's 1-skeleton based on the loom space's 1-skeleton, thereby providing a concrete outcome that may be useful for further investigation. This research was conducted in collaboration with Michael Yampolsky.

This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. We find that at the ILC (CLIC) with 8 ab$^{-1}$ (5 ab$^{-1}$), the discovery reach extends to combinations of the two leading HEFT coefficients with magnitudes of order $10^{-5}$ ($10^{-4}$). We also investigate the predicted rates for the four top jet signature without missing energy in the $b \bar b t \bar t$ final state and find that at the ILC (CLIC) with 8 ab$^{-1}$ (5 ab$^{-1}$), the discovery reach extends to combinations of the two leading HEFT coefficients with magnitudes of order $10^{-3}$ ($10^{-2}$). We conclude that future high-energy electron-positron colliders are predominantly sensitive to specific BSM Higgs couplings involving the pair production of heavy Higgs bosons, and that in the EFT framework, these couplings can be safely explored within a particular mass regime of the colliders' reach. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. However, fully explaining the anisotropy of drag requires more complex flow models that take into account the grain's high friction and the formation of sharp edges, and are yet to be developed. Nonetheless, our research found that the drag experienced by the cylinder is linked to the anisotropy of sediment transport, and that this anisotropy can be minimized when the grain's speed is similar to its depth. This phenomenon could be influential in a range of natural and industrial settings where sediment transport and flow play a key role. A comparable phenomenon has also been observed with a spherical solid moving through granular material, as reported previously. A mathematical model of this phenomenon has been proposed in the appendix of this paper. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. To further understand these findings, we analyzed the ratio of elliptical to triangular flow, $\frac{v_2}{v_3}$, finding it to be largely unaffected by centrality or particle type but displaying a gradual increase as transverse momentum increases. HSM models cannot solely account for our results, implying that triangular flow's centrality independence may be influenced by multiphase interactions. Moreover, our analysis incorporates measurements of $v_3$ for p+Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV and Ni+Ni collisions at 1.96 TeV for comparative purposes.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Additionally, this method's effectiveness is illustrated through specific PDE examples. By taking advantage of the flexibility of the GMRES algorithm and the ease of implementing additional costs for preserving properties, this study's results show that this approach is particularly beneficial for large systems, offering a practical and efficient solution to the challenge of property preservation. Lastly, this study's methodology can be applied to other Krylov solvers and other preservation properties, and suggests several potential avenues for future research. Lastly, this study provides numerical data available online. The author hopes this work will contribute to the ongoing efforts of the numerical analysis community in advancing time-stepping methods that preserve essential properties of the original solution. The paper is structured as follows: section 1 provides an introductory context; section 2 reviews the basic principles of Krylov solvers and preservation-based discretization techniques; section 3 discusses the limitations of existing schemes and the proposed modification of the GMRES algorithm; section 4 applies this modification to specific PDE examples; section 5 concludes the paper. The author dedicates this work to Professor Nick Gould, a pioneer in the field of large-scale nonlinear minimisation, and thanks several individuals who contributed to this research, provided valuable advice, and assisted with numerical experiments. The author also acknowledges the funding agencies that supported this work. The paper ends with a list of abbreviations used in the text. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online. The proposed method has numerous applications in laparoscopic liver surgery, as well as in radiotherapy and soft-tissue trauma analysis. The challenges faced in developing this method include balancing organ deformation hardness and softness, accurately defining boundary conditions, and adequately addressing noise in intraoperative surface data. The code developed in Python can be found at https://github.com/ghristenson/volume_surface_registration. The simulation datasets as well as real-world experimental data used in this research are available for use by others. The proposed network architecture has a relatively small amount of training data required, making it a scalable solution for complex soft-tissue navigation. In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets. We believe this model has vast potential applications in various IoT devices.

This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. Finally, we explore timely possibilities of integrating Timeloops with orchestration tools. The source code for Timeloops is currently available under the permissive BSD license on GitHub. The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. By leveraging our model's insights, coaches can gain a deeper understanding of these situations and make more informed tactical decisions, such as deploying specific players in particular scenarios. Ultimately, our system has the potential to be a key tool for teams looking to improve their performance in high-stakes situations. The model's performance has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/sfeng26/soccer-recommendation. The results of our research have been visualized in the paper and are available at https://sfeng26.github.io/soccer-recommendation. The InStat dataset used in the study is accessible upon request from the dataset owner. The paper is a submission for NIPS 2020. The code for the paper is a part of the package for the NIPS 2020 Reinforcement Learning and Game Theory Challenge and can be found at https://github.com/NYUMLResearch/RGL Challenge. The challenge organizers provided the code for the paper. The research was conducted without the financial support of any institution. The authors declare no conflict of interest. The paper is dedicated to Zhiyuan Liu. The dataset used in the study contains contextual information about actions taken during soccer matches, along with the outcomes of those actions, allowing for the development of a policy to optimize future actions based on the game state. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. These advancements pave the way for an exploration of the low-frequency part of the data, and combining this with the existing FWI framework is also suggested. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Moreover, such a design would permit easy transition 
between different TEM applications. Our proposed designs have been created and 
functional prototypes are ready for implementation on a TEM. The research has been 
conducting in collaboration with Oxford Instrument's Cryo-TEM. The proposed 
schemes could also be adaptable for other advanced phase plate techniques such as

Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Our analysis also explores the relationship between certain subgroups of G and the additive Galois module properties of rings of integers in K. Our research expands upon previous work of the same name by Leopoldt, and we provide counterexamples to a specific conjectural generalization of his results. Additionally, our findings include characterizations of certain rational group algebra modules that are invariant under the action of G and derive from properties of the distribution of ramified primes within the given extension. Lastly, our work involves an examination of the unique structures of submodules associated with prime ideals and their corresponding behavior under the action of G. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, our findings are applicable to other
neuroepithelial tissues exhibiting IKNM, and we show that the retinal ganglion cell layer's formation serves as a key
barrier in determining the random diffusion of nuclei and thus their random cell fate selection. Lastly, once the retinal
surface is fully populated, and once the overlying neural layer reaches a certain thickness, the system's behavior shifts,
and a distinct, non-random cell fate selection pattern emerges. This process is so gradual that it is difficult to
distinguish from diffusion-induced random cell fate selection; however, it is distinct from the system's initial diffusion
phase and may be related to the retino-temporal wave-like pattern observed in many visual systems. This study on the
retina provides a novel, insight-filled example of how random cell fate selection driven by diffusive forces alone can
lead to oriented patterns in neuroepithelial tissues during development. The underlying principles are likely applicable
to other visually organized systems developing from neuroepithelial tissues. The associated algorithms and analysis
methods are available online at https://www.github.com/NeuralMigration. The associated data is available online at

Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. This is accomplished by defining two degrees of continuity, a more general and a more specific version, and demonstrating their equivalent status in relation to computability. This is further elaborated in the form of an explicit example. This paper includes the original conference presentation along with additional results. This research was funded by the ANR Project SynCol and the INRIA Project Dumas. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. Unlike previous first-order representations, this formulation accounts for state changes over time as well as the worst-case effects of disturbances. Although this method produces a more accurate prediction of reachable states, the discretization of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation makes it less efficient and more difficult to implement compared to first-order methods. To overcome these limitations, we've introduced a new variant of the equation, called the Cauchy-type variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, which accounts for state changes and worst-case disturbances in a continuous and efficient manner. This new equation enables the calculation of reachable states without the need for the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation's discretization, and we've proven that this approach is equivalent to the original method for continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations. Furthermore, we've applied this new variant to a continuous time-linear system in the presence of disturbances, and demonstrated that it yields a solution that is directly related to the system's reachability matrix. In addition, we've developed a numerical scheme to solve the Cauchy-type variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, and validated this approach with comparative experiments against the Eulerian method and a direct simulation of the system. Finally, we've introduced a new metric for evaluating the accuracy of state estimation in uncertain environments, and demonstrated the efficacy of the Cauchy-type variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation in such contexts. A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures but also manifests in areas with strong magnetic fields. Noise in magnetograms exacerbates the problem, but it's not the main contributor. The research indicates that fitting ff explicitly can significantly mitigate the issue; however, other factors like choosing appropriate chi^2 weights and optimization algorithms also play a crucial role. Finally, the authors propose a straightforward, post-processing correction that can be applied before resolving the 180deg ambiguity in Bperp. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Our complex network's advantages are illustrated in simulations of the (3+1)D Hubbard model, a critical model thought to be relevant to superconducting phases found in certain materials, where we successfully keep the determinant cost linear while solving the self-consistent equation for the chemical potential required to tackle the sign problem. Furthermore, this method is shown to outperform the 'interaction expansion' in determining the determinant, a non-trivial assessment facilitated by the exact computation of the determinant in the compactified complex space. Our results are completed with simulations of the (3+1)D Hubbard model in the 'finite temperature' regime, a previously unexplored regime in this model, where temperature and strong interaction effects are compared. Our code is available at https://github.com/ComplexNetworkLab/ComplexNetworkLab.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code is available at https://github.com/HongSeokYou/DP-HyperParameterTuning. The paper concludes by highlighting the opportunities for further improvements in the low-resolution estimation of performance in private deep learning. The challenge of estimating the balance between privacy and performance accurately enough for effective hyperparameter tuning remains a major obstacle in the development of successful and widely applicable algorithms. The paper suggests five potential approaches for further research including the integration of transfer learning for effective hyperparameter tuning, the development of combined algorithms for Bayesian optimization and reinforcement learning, the integration of human expertise for hyperparameter tuning, the deployment of robust and efficient random search methods, and the development of techniques for estimating performance from gradient descent algorithms. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. The accuracy of the planned $H{\alpha}$ narrow-band observation dataset of planetary nebulae emitted light was enhanced by applying a more sensitive threshold for distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum, and the analysis of planetary nebulae frequency distributions across various mass ranges revealed a previously unknown factor that could potentially influence the calculation of distances to galaxies. The previously mentioned observation dataset and analytical findings suggest that the practical feasibility of conducting similar research on other galaxy clusters and groups is likely. The comprehensive database of planetary nebulae remains suitable for further scientific investigations, including velocity dispersion analysis, detailed chemical abundance assessments, and a comprehensive mapping of the galaxy structure. The discovered planatory nebulae and related data for the galaxies NGC 1316, NGC 1374, NGC 1379, NGC 1387, NGC 1394, NGC 1404, NGC 1407, and NGC 1419 are also being made publicly available. The most reliable estimated distance to the Fornax cluster based on planetary nebulae analysis combined with the surface brightness fluctuations method is 19.85 megaparsecs

Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. With its versatility and high-performance capabilities, LifeStream is suitable for multiple application domains, not just healthcare. The system's efficient design, combined with its open source nature, allows users to customize LifeStream to meet the unique requirements of their specific applications. The underlying engine architecture is also scalable, enabling easy integration with distributed stream processing frameworks. The source code for LifeStream is available at \url{https://github.com/StreamML/LifeStream}.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To demonstrate this, we employ a simple, adaptive strategy that yields results surpassing the performance of commonly used loss functions. Our work is applicable to a broad spectrum of problems, including federated learning,/shared classification models, and adaptive loss selection. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/EvalLoss.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. In particular, the proposed approach is applied to Gaussian minimum displacement CPM, resulting in previously unknown performance data. For this format, the best delay period is found to be $K=5$ with a 2.8dB performance gain at a 10^-3 error rate, compared to the optimal coherent detection system. Similar improvements are observed with binary differential detection. Despite its optimized performance, the research highlights the previously unknown fact that the commonly employed $K=2$ value yields a 2.5dB performance gain, nearly equivalent to the 2.8dB gain achieved with $K=5$. Consequently, this research delivers a versatile delay period framework that is applicable to numerous CPM formats, including Gaussian minimum displacement, Gaussian, map, and Martinian differentials. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  The comprehensive nature of ATOMIC is further underscored by our investigation into the underlying principles governing this dataset, and we highlight potential pathways for future research into the complex patterns of machine-based commonsense reasoning. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. The associated code is available at https://github.com/QCRM/NISQHHL. The research illustrates the potential of HHL in conjunction with actual Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware, leveraging simulation and actual-device execution of a portfolio-optimization case study involving the ML-CNN stock market. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This achievement is also observed when transferring knowledge to a related task, namely the Google speech recognition system. Moreover, the proposed model yields a 12.75% reduction in WER when trained with a much larger unpaired text dataset. This research was originally published in the conference paper: Speech-text based multi-modal training with bidirectional attention for improved speech recognition – ICML 2021, and the updated version in the conference paper: Bidirectional Attention Based Multi-Modal Speech Recognition – ICASSP 2022.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. The paper also discusses a simpler uniformized version of the weighted ballot theorem. The most significant contribution of this paper to the weighted ballot theorem is in showing that the sum of the first $k_n$ parking locations is asymptotically normal with a mean of $\frac{k_n}{2}$ and a variance of $\frac{k_n}{2}$ for $k_n$ growing faster than $\sqrt{n}$. The paper's findings can be interpreted as the weighted ballot theorem's uniformized version's deepened understanding, thereby providing a more subtle and complicated weighted ballot theorem scenario. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The observed effects also prompt a re-examination of the assumption that coherent quantum phase slips are the primary obstacle to conduction in these nanowires. The influence of the gate electrode on the superconducting properties of the nanowires is further explored by conducting measurements of the critical current distribution and the relation between the critical current and the barrier height, which provides valuable information about the material and the nanowire's geometry. The results presented here include the derivation of the relation between the critical current distribution and the barrier height, the determination of the average cross-sectional area of the nanowires, and the estimation of their average length. The discrepancy in the period shifts can be attributed to the presence of surface roughness and the resulting variation in the nanowires' length, which is confirmed by scanning electron microscopy images of the nanowires. The effects observed in the NbN nanowires share some characteristics with those seen in superconducting single-phase multiple-gap materials but exhibit distinct differences, prompting the assignment of a single energy gap for these nanowires. Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views. Our code is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghulam-pasha/NovelViewVP.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications. The scalability and versatility of this device concept were also highlighted. The capacity for arbitrary design and mode profile was demonstrated, enabling a vast range of photonic processing tasks, from interferometric sensing and signal routing to quantum information processing and photonic neural networks. The approach presented here offers a promising method for engineering non-trivial mode structures and spatial coupling in photonic devices, and the device itself can be utilized in a variety of settings including interference-based photonic processing, sensing and quantum computing. The development of a $2D$ photonic lattice was also described, which includes a range of complex configurations such as lattices with multiple beam splitters, magnetic lattices, and lattices with both global and local mode coupling. The spatial distribution of light can be manipulated by moving a laser beam within this lattice, enabling continuous tuning of the photonic device, and allowing for a wide range of applications including spatial mode conversion, photonic neural networks and quantum simulation. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. This conclusion is further supported by calculations of transport parameters based on average Cobalt and Bismuth properties. The study of larger Cobalt layers showed that the Hall effect returns to the intrinsic scattering type. The investigation also discovered a transition from skew to side-jump scattering of carrier spins as the Fermi level is shifted towards the Cobalt's 3d band edges. The research was conducted using a cobalt-bismuth multilayer without any surface modification, and the results demonstrate that the spin-orbit proximity effect and the associated increase in Anomalous Hall Resistivity can be quite substantial, offering promising applications in the control of Spin-Orbit Coupling and Hall effects in superconductor and semimetallic systems. The study further suggests that the effects observed in this research could be even more significant in systems with larger interface scattering. The science behind this research can be applied to other systems with strong spin-orbit coupling and may lead to the discovery of novel phases in materials such as graphene, ferromagnetic layers, and semimetallic systems. The findings of this research have been verified through extensive calculations of transport parameters based on cobalt and bismuth properties, and the results show that the effects observed in this research are fundamental and general, and the science behind this research can be applied to a wide range of materials and systems. This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations. The analysis indicates that the generalised Mie-type potential model offers an improved understanding of quantum systems, with physical properties such as scattering phase, energy eigenvalue, and bound state eigenfunction accurately calculated through the solution to the fractional Schrödinger equation. The paper also delves into the conceptual basis of the fractional Schrödinger equation and its relation to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. The application of the model to a diatomic molecule, with its energy eigenvalue calculated and compared to existing literature, showcases the generalized Mie-type potential's applicability to real-world quantum systems. The paper concludes by highlighting the significance of fractional derivatives in physics, with the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach demonstrated through the generalised Mie-type potential model. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. The development of our approach has implications for the development of more reliable neural networks, as it addresses concerns related to how neural networks overfit when they have access to vast amounts of data. The code for our approach can be found at: https://github.com/Onnet/NeuralNetworkLipschitzRegularisation.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. This work is part of ongoing efforts to study the possibilities of lepton-flavour non-universality in various processes, and the developed code has applications beyond ditau events. It can also be used to study other phenomena, such as pair productions of top quarks and ditau bosons, and is an enhancement of existing research on vector leptoquarks. To facilitate further studies, this code is made available for use by the scientific community.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. The code is available at https://github.com/yongchunyang/PMNet.

This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. The revised version of CT also provides insights into the structure of the texts that admit coherent connections between statements. The study concludes by examining the implications of these findings for the ideas underlying CT and the coherence of conversations. The study's methods and analysis are complex and rely on specialized terminology from centering theory and neural networks. The study focuses on characterizing the connections within the text and develops a new metric to describe these connections. The study finds that the connections within the text are determined by a linear combination of the coherence of the text and the similarity between successive statements. The study also examines the elements that contribute to the coherence of the text and finds that the relations within the text are ordered in a hierarchical pattern. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. In particular, this approach can be highly beneficial for medical research facilities like cancer treatment centers that demand high levels of reliability and can take advantage of the significant gains offered by multi-pass energy recovery linacs.

Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. In both limits, the two-gluon CEV maintains its complex colour structure, arising from a colour-ordered hexagon function that arises via colour-ordering kinematics. A notable finding under the MRK limit is that the two-gluon CEV simplifies to a level 2 BFKL equation predicted form, although with an important adjustment to the usual impact factor product structure.
