Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This indicates that even mild ribbons in longer wavelengths can contain extreme far-ultraviolet bright enough to significantly impact the UV environment of exoplanetary surfaces. This analysis provides a crucial tool for interpreting the level of UV radiation in bio-signature windows around low-mass stars and highlights the importance of considering the distribution of ribbons' flux spectra in exoplanetary habitability assessments. This research was conducted in partnership with the TESS Mission, Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, Boston University, Boston MA, and the University of Hawaii at Manoa, Honolulu HI.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. This work's contribution sits at the intersection of clustering, influence estimation, and data-driven identification, and the methodology offered is suitable for integrating with optimization and control frameworks. The associated code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Apidan/InfluenceClustering.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Moreover, we discover that each dimension of the sparse code corresponds to a specific linguistic element, and by analyzing these codes, we can identify the underlying structures of language. To further prove the versatility of sparse codes, we demonstrate how they can be utilized in a supplementary classification task, resulting in a notable improvement in classification accuracy. The code for SparseGAN is available at https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. Specifically, the open star cluster Caldwell 69 and the globular cluster NGC 6253 are identified as particularly promising case studies. Evidence supporting interstellar panspermia may be found by analyzing the distribution of life-bearing planets within these clusters, and could have far-reaching implications for a range of astrophysical and biological disciplines. Ultimately, detecting the presence of interstellar panspermia would also provide a means of transferring microbial life from one system to another, offering a means of extending life expectancy for individual stars before life becomes extinct in their universe.

Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Ultimately, our research delivers capture-recapture models that can be used by itself to analyze resource selection, and new models that integrate capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate population density, space usage, and resource selection simultaneously.  We apply and evaluate these methods with real data to demonstrate their functionality.  We also provide R code to facilitate implementation.  Our study discovered various encounter probability model specifications that minimize loss of information when using capture-recapture data to infer resource selection, and differentiable different encounter probability models that can be used with optimization methods to analyze space usage, and offers guidelines to reduce the number of capture locations required to estimate density and space usage correctly.  Our findings contribute to better capture-recapture analysis, resource selection analysis, and provide biologically meaningful interpretations of encounter probability models.  We discuss our results in the context of bear ecology. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. This research is also made relevant by comparing it to a modern context, such as conformal gravity. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. The underlying principles and concepts of this testing theory are presented in detail, starting from a simple and intuitive basis that gradually leads to the complex aspects of the method. This involves incorporating concepts like context and interference, as well as a sophisticated resolution mechanism that makes use of the geometric properties of a specific set of vectors. This testing method has been applied to real-world programs written in C, with notable successes in fixing issues found during testing. It is also available as a free online tool called the Geometric Testing Environment, which allows anyone to test its capabilities and experience its features for themselves. This testing method and environment are the result of the author's PhD research, conducted at the University of Oxford under the supervision of Dr. Keunmyung Kim and Dr. Ian Holmes.

Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ is then described as acting on the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$. This action results in the set's equivalence to the set defined by the root system $\Phi_0$. This implies that the set's invariants are determined by the invariants of the root system $\Phi$. Furthermore, the action of $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ on the set can be extended to the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{6}$. This extended action leads to the set's equivalence to the set defined by the root system $\Phi$. This in turn implies that the set's invariants are determined by the invariants of the root system $\Phi$. This further extends a previous result presented in the paper titled "Orbits of vectors in some representations. I". The action of the group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi, K)$ on the set can be obtained from the action of the group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ on the set by taking the projectivization of the action. This results in the set's equivalence to the set defined by the root system $\Phi$. This in turn implies that the set's invariants are determined by the invariants of the root system $\Phi$. This further extends a previous result presented in the paper titled "Orbits of vectors in some representations. I". The result presented in the paper titled "Orbits of vectors in some representations. I" can be considered as a special case of these results. The results presented in the paper titled "Orbits of vectors in some representations. I" were initially established using the result presented in the paper titled "The quantum group $U_q(g)$ and its operator algebra implementation" by V. Chari and R. Pressley

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The accuracy of the algorithm's size estimation is guaranteed by theoretical analysis, which establishes a lower bound on the accuracy of the estimate among the genuine nodes. Our investigation also establishes a benchmark for the task of network size estimation from local observations in networks containing a specified number of malicious nodes, specifically showing that the underlying problem is difficult to solve even for the most advanced computational models and cannot be achieved within a certain time frame or to a certain level of accuracy, no matter how small, unless the number of malicious nodes is bounded by a constant factor of the number of genuine nodes. Our most advanced achievement is a statistical argument validating the accuracy of the estimate generated by our algorithm among the genuine nodes, which serves as a crucial component in our investigation of the problem's difficulty and enables us to establish a lower bound on the task's complexity. Our research involves multiple novel technical innovations, specifically the introduction of a new random graph model, the development of a binary search algorithm, and the introduction of a statistical accuracy argument from scratch. Our investigation also involves an in-depth examination of the underlying challenges and the reasons why standard complex network models cannot be used to prove the difficulty of network size estimation from local observations. Our results involve a constant factor change to the model introduced in a related and prior study, specifically changing from a logarithmic scale to a scale defined by the logarithm of the logarithm, which enables us to extend the investigation to networks of a much larger size and provides a significantly stronger lower bound on the task's complexity

Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. The development of an advanced solver in conjunction with this approach enables the creation of high-quality initial data that meet precise simulation requirements, as shown in a study involving a superdense quark star. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. We find that the anomalous Nernst coefficient in Mn$_3$NiN exhibits a 5.5-fold enhancement when subjected to a lateral pressure, which we attribute to the deformation-induced changes in crystal structure and resulting effects on the electronic band structure and magnetic arrangement. This novel interaction offers a means of controlling the anomalous Nernst coefficient and potentially other phenomena related to ferromagnetism and thermal transport. Next, we demonstrate that lateral pressure can be utilized to manipulate the anomalous Nernst effect across other antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials, ending with a discussion on the implications for experimental and theoretical studies of these materials.

We have derived improved differentiability properties for solutions to a non-autonomous obstacle problem, formulated as
  \begin{equation*}
  \min \left\{\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx\,:\, v\in
  \mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right\}.
  \end{equation*} Given the growth restrictions imposed on the function $f$, with respect to the gradient variable, we find that when the obstacle function is bounded and satisfies certain regularity conditions, the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ being part of the Sobolev space, leads to a corresponding increase in the differentiability of the solution, provided the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ belongs to a $W^{1, p+2}$. Notably, we address subquadratic growth conditions on the function $f$, i.e., where $f(x,\xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ and $1<p<2$ and map $a$ also belongs to a Sobolev space, where $\Omega$ and $x,\xi\in \Omega$. Additionally, when considering the associated parabolic problem, we obtain enhanced regularity properties for the solution, where the differentiability index increases to three, i.e., from $C^{1+\alpha}\left(0,T;W^{1,\gamma}(\Omega)\right)$ to $C^{2+\alpha}\left(0,T;W^{1,\gamma}(\Omega)\right)$. In both cases, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the solution with these heightened regularity properties. Lastly, we provide a relevant example that demonstrates the subquadratic growth condition is indeed necessary.

Lastly, this approach can be extended to the infinite coefficient field case, as shown in the appendix written by E. H. Yang. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The proposed method can be applied to a wide range of projects that utilize composite materials, from aerospace to sports equipment. 
Furthermore, by utilizing conductivity rather than resistance, a novel conductivity-based EIT reconstruction technique was developed, offering a better understanding of composite material conductivity and facilitating the development of more realistic physical models. 
The proposed technique can also detect type of damage by analyzing conductivity distributions, as demonstrated in the case of holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The integration of EIT with genetic algorithms and physical models can be applied to other detection techniques and projects that involve composite materials, aerospace projects, and sports equipment design. 
The proposed technique can also be developed for real-time applications, as well as for monitoring changes in material conductivity over time, as shown in the case of CNF-GFRP composites left outside in harsh environmental conditions. 
The proposed project can be a starting point for a range of new research projects, as well as industrial collaborations with companies that manufacture composite materials, sports equipment, and aerospace projects. 
The proposed technique can also be developed for other self-sensing materials, as well as for detecting types of damage in composite materials, such as delamination, fractures, and cracks. 
The proposed technique can be a starting point for a range of new research projects, as well as industrial collaborations with companies that manufacture composite materials, sports equipment, and aerospace projects.

We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures. This conveys that these lattices have finitely many conjugacy classes of torsion elements. Moreover, this leads to the conclusion that they contain a subgroup isomorphic to a biautomatic group with finite index. Finally, by extending the concept of biautomaticity to graph groups, we show that a specific class of graph groups are biautomatic, resulting in the same outcomes mentioned above for their associated uniform lattices. This study builds upon previous work by Bestvig, Davis, and Drutu, who initially established the biautomatic nature of a specific class of groups, and Hauser and Schreier, who investigated the concept of biautomaticity within the context of lattice groups. The paper also includes an analysis of the relationship between biautomaticity and other group properties, such as finiteness and hyperbolicity, as well as a discussion on the outcome for specific groups, such as right-angled lattices based on complete graphs and trees. Furthermore, we provide a characterization of biautomatic uniform lattices and present an approach to establishing the biautomatic nature of a group by verifying the biautomatic nature of its subgroup of stable letters. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of this ECoG-based BCI in recovering autonomous walking in individuals with spinal cord injuries at different levels of mobility. Although limited to this specific case study, the underlying technology presents a platform for exploring other complex neural activities in various applications. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Lastly, our model's flexibility enables seamless integration into existing systems, offering a simple solution for transferring static graphs to their dynamic equivalents. We publicly release DECENNT's code and DECENNT-generated graphs for magnetic resonance imaging data.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. This discovery has implications for fields like herpetology and entomology, where the hidden movement of animals in still images could be uncovered, along with applications in filmmaking, animation, and video filtering. A related video demo is available at https://youtu.be/2HfLwD4MwGk.

In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. The paper also includes a discussion on the relationship between the NN and other classical iterative methods, as well as an analysis of the NN's stability and theoretical bound on convergence. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The analysis covers a wide range of mass scenarios, with special focus on the effective field theories used in low-energy regimes. The findings have been used to interpret direct detection constraints on the parameter space of the MSSM. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. One approach builds upon a previous finding by K. Berankiewicz, J. McMillan, and M. Singer, and the second method leverages the Chinese Remainder Theorem and properties of prime powers to derive the result. Both approaches enable us to enumerate all possible instances where $a$ and $b$ meet this condition. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both of these scenarios are subsets of a broader group defined by the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, which can also be expressed as the product of two polynomials of degree one. This polymeric form enables us to solve the equation for a specific constraint on the value of $n$, and in doing so, we obtain a second-degree equation in the variable $n$. This resulting equation, known as the "norm equation", enables us to determine the values of $n$ that satisfy the original condition, and thereby extend the validity of a previous result proved by S. Chowdhury, M. Leinartias, and G. Targaitchiew. Additionally, we establish a relationship between the values of $a$ and $b$ that satisfies the norm equation, and thereby derive a third-degree equation in the variable $n$. This latter equation, which we call the "primitive norm equation", enables us to determine all values of $n$ that satisfy the original condition, and thereby extend the validity of a previous result proved by Chowdhury et al. We demonstrate how to solve the primitive norm equation using a method we call the " ladder method", which involves a series of successive extensions to the original equation, each of a higher degree than the last. This generalisation involves a further concept we call the "universal norm equation", which enables us to derive the primitive norm equation from the universal norm equation using a method we call the "conversion process", and thereby solve the universal norm equation. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Additionally, this approach was applied to a more complex scenario in which the robot navigated a soft surface to reach a high platform. This project's findings have implications for legged locomotion on soft ground and provide a feasible control system for future applications. It has been concluded that a combination of RFT and feedback control can be an effective way to control robots on soft ground. Additionally, this approach has been successfully utilized in novel scenarios, such as ratchet hopping and ramp climbing, that are related to legged locomotion on soft ground. It has been observed that a ratchet hopping movement is more energy-efficient than traditional hopping movements. A discussion on the issues related to this project, along with its advantages and limitations, has been presented. Moreover, some novel scenarios, along with their MATLAB simulations, have been shown in the appendix. Finally, this project can serve as a starting point for further research and development of control systems for robots moving on soft ground. In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values. A comparison is also made with results obtained using the heavy quark limit and the heavy meson effective theory. Moreover, the connection between the contact interaction scheme and the heavy quark limit is clarified by a parameter transformation, which facilitates the determination of the interaction strength required for heavy quark limit equivalence. The results presented hold for a range of gap parameter values and illustrate how the ground-state properties of mesons rely on the gap parameter and consequently, on the number of quark flavors. This knowledge is pertinent to the study of meson form factors in the heavy quark limit and the contact interaction scheme. The findings obtained can be applied to a unified scheme studying the properties of mesons, which includes both light and heavy quark compositions. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. HDTM generates hierarchies by identifying latent topics that correspond to specific network nodes, thereby ensuring the resulting models align with the original network structure. We also developed an enhanced version of HDTM, DeepHDTM, which incorporates a neural network-based extension to further improve performance and scalability. Despite its advanced features, both models demonstrate the ability to handle extremely large datasets, with HDTM achieving notable results on Wikipedia's full content while showcasing the benefits of a non-parametric approach. In our evaluation of HDTM on Wikipedia, we found that the model excels at aligning with the original network, accurately identifying nodes that correspond to the proposed hierarchies, with an average node matching score of 0.261, and significantly outperforms a leading baseline in various metrics, as shown in our experiments using three smaller datasets. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Despite the artificially generated nature of these simulations, the results hold significant value in demonstrating the practical applicability of quench dynamics to quantum annealing protocols. The current study focuses on the precise cover problem, although the underlying principles can be applied to other combinatorial optimization problems following a similar scenario. The methodology presented herein offers a concrete means of interpreting quench data in the context of quantum annealing, as well as a valuable tool for validating various theoretical models that simulate quantum annealing and quench dynamics. The study further highlights the pivotal role of initial condition averaging, which is crucial for obtaining accurate results from quench simulations, particularly when analyzing complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. The findings presented herein can be replicated using various quench and annealing simulation platforms, cementing their general applicability. The quantum annealing gap and quench dynamics are interconnected through the average overlap between the initial state and the post-quench Hamiltonian's eigenstates, which directly relates to the annealing gap's functional behavior. The current research demonstrates that the average overlap can be determined from the quench data, thereby providing a quantitative understanding of the annealing gap's behavior and, by extension, the efficiency of quantum annealing protocols. The study further explores the connection between the average overlap and initial state preparation, revealing that the average overlap can be influenced by modifying the initial state, which in turn affects the annealing gap

Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Ultimately, our comprehensive analysis highlights the intricate relationships
between weight transfer, screening, and the motion of electrons as well as the
robust emergence of $d$-wave pairing in this specific model. 
Despite the intricate details, our findings also demonstrate that one-band
approximations are capable of accurately capturing the essential properties of
infinite layered nickelates, which should be applicable to experiments involving
Lanthanum/Nickelate interfaces. 
Lastly, our research underscores the significance of considering weight transfer
and screening in two-band models, which could provide valuable insights for a
variety of other material science investigations. 
In the process of studying infinite layered nickelates, we discovered that the
phenomenon of weight transfer and screening is so fundamental that it demands
investigation in its own right, which has been demonstrated through a
quantum Monte Carlo evaluation of a simple two-band model involving both strong
correlations and motion of electrons. 
This further revealed the intricate relationships between movement of electrons,
screening, weight transfer, and the electron configuration, which in turn
affected the ground state state and pairing symmetry, resulting in both $s$-wave
and $d$-wave pairing

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.  This prediction can be tested by various models of the hadron-quark phase transition, reflecting the complexity of quark phase transitions and the underlying physics of dense matter.  This framework can be applied to heavy ion collisions and quark-gluon plasma research, as well as to the study of compact stars and two-solar mass neutron stars.  If confirmed, this expectation could mark the overthrown of the Barrabes-Price barrier in the context of quark star radii.  This prediction also predicts that strange quark stars exist within a specific density range, with radii between 10.5 to 12.8 km, offering a distinctive signature that could be distinguished from neutron or hybrid stars through the analysis of pulsar spectra.  This could potentially result in the discovery of strange quark stars, thus providing conclusive evidence for the deconfinement phase transition and revealing the sound velocity's detailed behavior in dense matter.  This prediction can be tested through a variety of models of the hadron-quark phase transition, reflecting the complexity of quark phase transitions and the underlying physics of dense matter.  This finding encourages the use of pulsar radius measurements in heavy ion collisions and quark-gluon plasma research, as well as in the study of compact stars and two-solar mass neutron stars.  If confirmed, this expectation could mark the overthrown of the Barrabes-Price barrier in the context of quark star radii.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. We have also demonstrated that constant scalar curvature ensures the stability of solutions to a particular optimization problem, which in turn leads to the consistency of a specific gradient flow. Furthermore, we have derived an expression for the second variation of an operator that is constantly zero, which will be useful in examining the behavior of the gradient flow near the critical point. This result has implications for certain types of manifolds, specifically those with bounded distance from a particular cone-like structure and compactly generated topological space, and provides an alternative proof of an existing theorem from Harmond's work. Additionally, we have established that harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate can be represented as a combination of surface area measures and radial Schur functions, which are characterized by their own derivative equation. This research was conducted in collaboration with H. Chen, X. Liang, and J. Zheng.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. The code for this approach is available at https://github.com/ghrua/CoarseToCareful.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. The proposed method is further extended to heterogeneous data sets in multi-parameter learning settings. The feasibility of the algorithm and its sensitivity to various parameters are demonstrated through simulations and real-world experiments. The proposed method has been implemented as an open source software available on GitHub. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  The findings support expanding access to mental health treatment for offenders within the justice system.  The research also accounts for various potential biases and finds that receiving mental health treatment reduces future crimes even when comparing similar offenders who were sentenced to incarceration instead.  The study identifies key factors that influence outcomes and finds that mental health treatment reduces future crimes more significantly for offenders who were sentenced to longer prison terms. Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. Specifically, we investigate the GMLE of $\eta_G$ as the mixing distribution $G$ and the distribution of the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ when the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Additionally, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ can be achieved using the profile likelihood method and the Newton-Raphson algorithm to update the initial guess of the GMLE. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing. We also provide a concise tutorial on building own models using PyKT at the associated research page. We encourage users to thoroughly examine our research results and model performances on different datasets, and to cite this work if they decide to use our findings in their own work. We anticipate PyKT and our research results will guide further improvements in deep learning knowledge tracing. We also open-source PyKT at https://github.com/pykt-team/pykt. We welcome industry partners and organizations operating in the educational technology sector to join us in validating and testing PyKT against their specific needs. We believe that the challenges we encountered in our research can be beneficial to other domains beyond educational knowledge tracing, where user data is used to guide modeling decisions. We propose a new term called Knowledge Tracing Quality, and we believe it can be applied to other domains such as conversational summarization and question answering. We propose a set of metrics to evaluate Knowledge Tracing Quality, including the presence of label dependence in validation sets, the presence of performance inflation due to label leakage in evaluation sets, the presence of bias in model performance across different subgroups, and the presence of overfitting in models. We also propose a methodology to detect hidden biases in models through reverse engineering. Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Specifically, it is shown that there exists a locally integrable function $X \in L^2(M)$ such that the distribution $X_\delta$, defined by the product of $X$ and any smooth function $\delta$, satisfies the properties of having compact support and being part of $C^\infty(M)$. Consequently, it follows that $C^{\infty}(M)$ contains a dense subset comprised of functions with compact support, which in turn implies that $C^{\infty}(M)$ is equivalent to the space of distributions with compact support, denoted as $C^\infty(M)'$. This result is further utilized to demonstrate that the existence of a continuous inverse to $P$ leads to the validity of the Helmholtz decomposition for any function in $L^2(M)$. This, in turn, implies that the existence of a continuous inverse to $P$ is equivalent to the validity of the Helmholtz decomposition for the manifold $M$. This result can be realized through either the use of differential forms or the use of tensors. This also includes the specific case of Riemannian manifolds. This research paper builds upon the results established by the authors in their previous paper, where it was demonstrated that the existence of a continuous inverse to $P$ leads to the validity of the Helmholtz decomposition for the compact manifold $M$. This previous result was further generalized to the case of manifolds with boundary by the authors in their paper titled: On the Helmholtz decomposition in non-compact manifolds with boundary. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our optimal model achieved a 14% reduction in WER compared to the baseline. We also investigated other related techniques for which we found only minor improvements. Notably, we found that Czech-English translation models did not produce high-quality results, with a lot of inaccuracies particularly in pronunciations. We suggest using targets with less linguistic differences to enhance transfer learning outcomes. Our code has been made available at this link https://github.com/martiniusz/CZ_Encoder_Teacher_for_CZ_Speaker.

To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/ghrua/sentence-metadata-network.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, through our investigation, we also established the existence of a mechanism with two agents that, for any possible values, has pure Nash equilibria inducing allocations that are fair up to any good and satisfy max-min fairness, although this mechanism is not efficient or strategy-proof. Lastly, we established the existence of a mechanism with two agents that, for any possible values, has pure Nash equilibria inducing allocations that are fair up to one good, as well as satisfying a certain rotation condition, although this mechanism is not efficient or strategy-proof. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The anomalous behavior of its stars also supports the conclusion that UGC 8839 has experienced a significant gravitational encounter in the distant past. The resulting stability of its disk has allowed the galaxy to maintain its extended structure despite the approach of cosmic acceleration due to the expanding universe. The decline in size of its disk over time is reflected in the younger age of the stars in its inner regions. The HII regions in UGC 8839 are concentrated at specific distances from a central point, possibly linked to the flanking presence of a massive satellite galaxy that has been tidally stripped. The disappearance of this satellite likely led to the galaxy's isolated state, contributing to the external pressure decrease that allowed the disk to stabilize further. The combination of its stable disk, rare HII distribution, and concentrated star formation makes UGC 8839 an outstanding example of a "faint spiral galaxy". The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Specifically, we test the validity of these predictions in situations where the quark mass approaches the mass of the threshold for breaking up a pion into two kaons. The results also shed light on the underlying physics of the I=2 pion amplitude system, which has been misunderstood until now. The study relies on data from multiple lattice simulations with the root-mean-square physical spacing of 0.085 fm, involving two flavors of dynamical quarks with a small mass and two different masses for the fourth quark flavor. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI-Education/SIT.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Specifically, our evaluation showed a 23% decrease in DSC values compared to BHHC, a 21% decrease compared to ACWC, and a 26% decrease compared to LCCC in both 2D and 3D scenarios. Additionally, our network's capture range was significantly broader, with a 2D DSC value exceeding 0.75 for all dataset samples. We further tested our model on 50 prostate images with varying field sizes and distances between megavoltage images, obtaining comparable results. All code has been made publicly available on GitHub at the time of submission. We believe our model meets these needs, offering a straightforward and accurate registration method using minimal training data. In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that single-particle entanglement can be optimized for implementing the steering phenomenon, which significantly enhances its capability to achieve non-local effects. Consequently, single-particle entanglement holds immense potential in generating non-local effects between distant locations, thereby making it an ideal resource for numerous quantum applications, including secure communication and quantum computation. Finally, we propose an experiment that can validate our findings by analyzing the spreading of the entangled wave function during the Stern-Gerlach experiment using a trapped cold atom. This experiment can be carried out using the existing infrastructure of various research groups around the world. In conclusion, our discovery of the intrinsic non-locality of single-particle entanglement, coupled with its spread and versatility, underscores its significance as a primal resource for implementing the phenomenon of steering in various quantum systems. In addition, this finding opens up numerous possibilities for single-particle entanglement in multiple settings, ranging from quantum thermodynamics to time-standard quantum systems. In particular, we propose utilizing single-particle entanglement to generate quantum coherence in open systems, which can be achieved by utilizing single-particle entanglement to influence the temperature of a harmonic oscillator in a quantum heat engine. In this process, single-particle entanglement results in the formation of coherent oscillations between the harmonic oscillator and a two-level system, which can be detected by analyzing the time-dependent energy

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios. This paper is tailored for researchers and experts in the fields of artificial intelligence, automotive technology, cryptography, and learning systems. This survey is also suitable for readers interested in general information about Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning in IoVs. This review is further reflected in a detailed chart outlining various BC-Enabled FL scenarios, challenges, and future research opportunities in IoVs. This chart can be utilized by practitioners and researchers for problem-solving and future project development. This paper concludes with a discussion on future research directions and possible BC-Enabled FL scenarios for IoVs. This includes possibilities for vehicle network data management, improved security and privacy preservation through Federated Learning, and various other applications. This has the potential to drive technological innovation and advance the development of IoVs. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.
