A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Scalar coding gain amounts to 2dB relative to traditional approaches, with 10dB relative gain in pilot data transmission. Moreover, this method demonstrates superiority with low-resolution transmitters. The proposed technique's effectiveness is proven through simulations.

A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to the heat flux direction has been lacking in scientific knowledge since its one-dimensional counterpart was discovered. A setup for realizing these currents on a three-dimensional cubic lattice has been devised by coupling a Hofstadter model to two separate heat baths of varying temperatures. Research demonstrates that the robustness of these currents can withstand various imperfections and tilting within certain nonequilibrium conditions. Additionally, boundary currents with robust stability were found, and the condition of being three-dimensionally robust indicates they require tunneling capabilities across all three spatial dimensions. The model exhibits robust surface currents applicable to both bosons and fermions, and the mechanisms of discrete symmetries were found to significantly contribute to the surface currents' stability. The study has further implications, with the finding that the stability of surface currents is directly linked to cubical lattice structures, and that it cannot be replicated on a one-dimensional chain due to the inherent lack of spatial dimensions. The research has been complemented by numerical simulations of actual experiments that can realize these surface currents, along with specific recommendations for optimizing the robustness of these currents through suitable tuning of the Hofstadter model, and for replicating the proposed quantum states in actuality. The discovery of robust surface currents on a three-dimensional lattice can lead to breakthroughs in the study of non-equilibrium states and may also have applications in the development of robust quantum metrology systems. The model has been made publicly available on the iQEstor website. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our study highlights the significance of searching for these mergers in the course of current and upcoming gravitational wave telescopes, particularly in their most sensitive optimal range of 5-7 Gpc^-1 year. The electrical magnetic field generated by these mergers, although weak, may also have implications for the formation of Population III star clusters. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate the effectiveness of this accelerated platform, we conducted a series of tests using both simple and complex evaluation methods and found that future text-based challenges will need significant improvements to break the current performance barrier. 
The streamlined version of these games, known as TextWorldExpress, is now available at https://github.com/TextWorldExpress.

The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The dissolution of these vortices usually occurs in the fall, but the extent of this phenomenon is yet to be studied. The termination of the north polar vortex is marked by the formation of strong cyclonic currents in the middle latitudes. The persistence of the southern hemisphere vortex was observed throughout the entire mission, unless it was obstructed by aerosol clouds. The reduction in size of the southern hemisphere vortex became visible in the late fall, but it was not until the winter that it started to break apart. The formation of the polar vortices in both hemispheres occurs at the same rate, with the difference lying in the duration of their existence. The vortex in the south existed for six to seven years, while the vortex in the north existed for four to five years. The discovery of a previously unknown wave that affects temperatures in the middle latitudes of Saturn's atmosphere is a significant finding from this research. The detailed analysis of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex has also revealed the intricate processes that govern the formation and dissolution of the polar vortices in both hemispheres. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. It is essential to note that this paper's results rely on the assumption that the nonlinearity does not contribute to the conserved charge associated with the symmetry of the Schrödinger equation, thereby preventing the formation of standing waves as solutions. The optimal blow-up criterion in this context remains an open problem. The approach employed in this study also yields a second consequence regarding the absence of bounded solutions in this context. The paper further cites previous works by Bizoń, Duncan, Glamba, Jensen, Katam, Lunardi, Nakamura, Oh, Schlenker, Simard, Tahra, Tohkan, Tohkan, and Zhou as references on specific cases. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/lingua-terra/MCSE.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. The code for FedSA is available at https://github.com/lingyu-93/FedSA.

We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank varies in different quartic fields for a fixed elliptic curve. Notably, under specific conditions, we establish the existence of an infinite number of $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve doesn't increase compared to its rank over the rational numbers. This achievement is made possible by our development of methods to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within certain quadratic fields, enabling control of the rank in families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions. Notably, in the $A_4$ case, we demonstrate that the rank growth is limitless. Our study also reveals strategies for identifying the 2-Selmer ranks of elliptic curves within specific quartic fields, and provides combinatorial results on the classification of $S_4$ quartic extensions, equivalent to classifying the division fields of a given genus-one curve over the rational numbers. Our methods are applicable to quartic extensions in the Galois group $T_4 \supseteq S_4$, offering a more general version of the Diophantine Arithmetic Lemma. Our work is motivated by the recent progress made by Gross, Kuo, and Taylor and also builds upon the previous results obtained by Goldstein, Heath-Brown, Parent, and Goldstein-Parent. Our results share some commonality with the results obtained by Gross, Kuo, and Taylor and also with those obtained by Parent and Goldstein-Parent. A crucial boundary, the quantum null energy condition, is used to measure the change in a region's entanglement entropy along a null direction in order to understand the quantum thermodynamics of complex systems. Investigating whether the quantum null energy condition limits irreversible entropy generation during quenching driven by an influx of energy and momentum from an infinite, memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories, our research finds that an increase in both entropy and temperature, as required by the classical Clausius inequality, is necessary to prevent a violation of the quantum null energy condition, specifically in quenching transitions that result in changes in thermal states dual to Banados-Teitelboim-Zanelli geometries. Additionally, our research provides lower and upper bounds for the change in entropy or temperature for a specific change in temperature or entropy in any initial state. Furthermore, our results indicate that the null energy condition is never overstepped in time and that the asymptotic rates can be determined analytically. Our study demonstrates that the entanglement entropy within a region of a specific length, $l$, eventually reaches a steady-state within a time frame of $l/2$ with an exponential decay rate of $3/2$, and that the coefficient for the quadratic growth of entanglement in time can be found for any $l$, and that the asymptotic rate of growth for a semi-infinite interval is directly proportional to the difference of the entropy densities of the initial and final states, along with determining the upper and lower limits for these rates of growth. Our findings are validated by comparing them to established results, such as the rates of growth for a semi-infinite interval with an change in temperature or entropy in the thermal state, or an change in temperature or entropy for a semi-infinite interval with an change in thermal state. Our research introduces a novel approach for calculating the time-dependent change in entropy or temperature for a semi-infinite interval with an change in thermal state, along with providing a holographic perspective on the relationship between the quantum null energy condition, the change in entropy or temperature for a semi-infinite interval with an change in thermal state, and the change in thermal state itself. Our findings are relevant for the hypothesis that the growth of entanglement is always bounded and provide a physical interpretation for the QNEC inequality in terms of the rate of growth of entanglement or the rate of change of thermal state parameters. We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. This research also leads to an investigation of the relationship between different measures of qubit state asymmetry, including their connection to the minimum time to release a system and the system-environment asymmetry in the Landau-Zener problem. A notable finding is that the optimal time to release a system is directly proportional to the largest eigenvalue of its density matrix, whereas in the Landau-Zener problem, this time is equal to half the spectral gap of the Hamiltonian, and is independent of the initial state. Moreover, another important result is that the minimal time to release a system can be determined by examining the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian's spectral smoothing operator, providing a more general and versatile approach. Finally, this work also involves an investigation of the quantum speed limit in the Bloch ball, leading to a crucial finding that the optimal state evolution pathway is along the radius of the Bloch sphere, and that the minimum time to release a system is equal to half the time it takes for a state to evolve from one point on the sphere to another. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. This study highlights the potential of integrated quantum elements, combining multiple materials, to serve as quantitative proxies for research on material flaws causing decoherence. This terahertz approach can be expanded to examine other quantum systems, such as Josephson junctions and ferroelectric quantum circuits. This work is also relevant to microwave engineering, facilitating the assessment of devices like microwave filters and resonators used in various applications. This research was conducted using facilities available at the Leipzig Institute for Solid-State Physics, and the results have been published in the journal npj Quantum Information.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This work is tailored to contribute to the ongoing discussion within the scientific community and to guide future research and potential missions to study the planet's interior, surface, and atmosphere, with the long-term goal of understanding the dynamics of terrestrial planet evolution.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. One example, subthreshold neuronal activity, is presented as an application of our methods. It is shown that the Bayesian estimator correctly infers the existence of either excitatory or inhibitory connections between neurons, in a real recording of neuronal activity. It is worth noting that the approach and results we have obtained can be extended to nonlinear Hawkes process models with time-varying parameters, as well as multivariate versions of these models. One issue with nonparametric Bayesian estimation is that it involves selecting the number of knots or nodes for the nonparametric baseline model, which is another significant result of our research. It has been found that based on the number of arrivals within a fixed time frame, the number of nodes in the model follows a parametric distribution, which in turn enables the selection of this number using the posterior predictive loss. It has been further discovered that the number of nodes is directly related to the intensity of the point process, which in turn enables the estimation of the intensity, as well as the selection of the number of nodes, using the posterior predictive intensity, according to the distribution of the number of nodes, as well as the distribution of the location of each node. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. If the input laser pulse contains a significant amount of elliptical polarization, the waveplate can maintain this inherent property while still increasing the peak power of the dominant component, which has also been demonstrated numerically. This indicates that the plasma waveplate is a highly versatile component that can be applied in a wide range of high-power laser pulse applications. This concept has been applied to a Chirped Pulse Amplification (CPA) system, where a $20\text{ PW}$ laser pulse capacity can be achieved with a relatively compact length of $10.5\text{ m}$. This involves a sophisticated analysis of the system's performance, including a detailed evaluation of the required plasma waveplate parameters, along with a comparison to an alternative solid-state waveplate based on birefringence, which could reach the same level of capacity but with a much longer laser system, of about $70\text{ m}$. This research highlights a groundbreaking finding of a $4\text{ PW}$ laser pulse with an extremely high degree of spatial uniformity, achieved through the combination of a properly designed plasma waveplate and a CPA system, which could reach the $20\text{ PW}$ level with a slightly longer plasma waveplate required. This involves a detailed investigation of the plasma waveplate's impact on the laser pulse, including a temporal and a spatial analysis, along with a discussion on the basic principles of a CPA system and the required parameters to achieve this level of performance. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. In contrast, a random error matrix can be corrected with a high probability of at least 1 - p^n, where p is the code's parameter and n is the matrix dimension. The proposed decoding structures also reveal an interesting relationship between the code's parameters and the rank of the error matrix. In the case of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half, our results specifically confirm an earlier proposed criterion of error correctability. Moreover, our analysis yields a tightened bound on the probability of correcting a random error matrix. The method we use for decoding a single error matrix can be further used to correct a random error matrix through a combination of this method and a switching strategy. This combined method is efficient, easy to implement, and provides a significant performance enhancement over the baseline uniform decoding method. The proposed decoding structures can be implemented using the rank metric encoding system's original parameters, without any need for additional design changes. In addition, we investigate the relationship between the code's rates, its parameter, and the error matrix's rank, and provide a solution graph that can be used to determine the code's ability to correct a particular rank of error matrix. The proposed decoding method can be applied to the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half, and our results confirm an earlier proposed criterion of error correctability, as well as providing a tightened bound on the probability of correcting a random error matrix. The method we use for decoding a single error matrix can be further used to correct a random error matrix through a combination of this method and a switching strategy. The code's ability to correct a particular rank of error matrix can be determined from the solution graph, without any need for additional design changes. The proposed decoding method provides a significant performance enhancement over the baseline uniform decoding method. The method we use for decoding a single error matrix is efficient and easy to implement, and provides a low-complexity solution to the decoding problem

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework rather than the AdS$_3$ framework. Moreover, this new perspective enables a direct link between the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation and massless higher-spin fields in the AdS$_3$ framework, facilitated by the HKLL bulk field reconstruction method. By harnessing this new picture, we are able to derive a closed-form expression for the four-point conformal block involving spinning primary fields as a product of two AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagrams. This resulting expression can be compared to the original integral representation of the spinning conformal block operator in CFT$_2$. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this new perspective on spinning conformal block operators extends to inclusive quantity measurements in CFT$_2$. These findings emerge from the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation of spinning primary fields and can be interpreted through the lens of the AdS$_3$ bulk field reconstruction, allowing for the explicit computation of inclusive quantity measurements in CFT$_2$ via the AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagrams. This research was initially presented in the form of an abstract at the 13th Conference on Quantum Field Theory under the influence of an External Field, held in Moscow, Russia, from the 25th to the 29th of June, 2018. These findings have also been presented in the form of an abstract at the 69th York Meeting of the AustMS, held in Melbourne, Australia, from the 26th to the 30th of June, 2017. This research has further been presented in the form of an abstract at the 68th Seminar of the Section of Theoretical Physics of the University, held in Moscow, Russia, from the 4th to the 8th of July, 2016. This research has also been presented in the form of an abstract at the Loops '16 Meeting, held in Sydney, Australia

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. Additionally, we explore the connection between combinatorial Pontrjagin classes and their differentiable counterparts via a topological transformation, establishing a relationship that is both intrinsic and dependent on the choice of combinatorial differentiable structure. Furthermore, we provide a proof of the equivalence between combinatorial and differentiable Pontrjagin classes via a non-singular transformation, thereby extending the results of Gelfand and MacPherson to a broader context. This extension is particularly notable as it encompasses the case of combinatorial and differentiable spin manifolds. We also examine the implications of this extension on the Stiefel-Whitney classes of a manifold. The development of our arguments involves employing classical ideas from the subject matter, such as the concept of orientable cover and Lefshmidt equality, as well as more advanced techniques like the use of subcomplexes in simplicial theory and the construction of suitable spaces from combinations of certain simplicial spaces. The relationship between combinatorial and differentiable spin manifolds is found to be equivalent to the validity of certain divisibility conditions related to the Pontrjagin-Hirzebruch $\sigma$-orientation and 38-fold cover of a manifold, providing a novel and significant result in its own right. We also provide a comparative examination of these conditions and their associated consequences on the structure of the manifold, along with a discussion of the specific case of 6-dimensional manifolds and the implications of our results for the existing literature on the subject. The development of our methods and the modification of those of Gelfand and MacPherson allow us to derive a simplified and more general formulation of their formula for Pontrjagin classes, as well as to extend and refine the results of other researchers such as the combination of the Stiefel-Whitney and Pontrjagin classes of a manifold and the validity of certain divisibility conditions related to the $\sigma$-orientation and 38-fold cover of a manifold. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. Nonetheless, SN~2020jfo exploded with a high energy explosion mechanism similar to other SNe~II, and its low luminosity is attributed to a relatively small mass loss rate during the plateau phase. The observed decline rate in the nebular-phase spectra is slower than expected, which may be influenced by the presence of a massive hydrogen envelope or the shell burning layer. The reduction in post-shock exponential temperature decline rate is higher than expected, which is consistent with the presence of hydrogen in the radiative layer. The observed nebular-phase spectra of SN~2020jfo are similar to those of SNe~II with a longer plateau duration, which may indicate that Type II supernovae with short plateau durations have diverse post-shock exponential temperature decline rates. The absence of a prominent [Ca~II] line in SN~2020jfo's nebular-phase spectra is also noted, which may be linked to a lower metallicity in the progenitor. The extensive recovery of SN~2020jfo's photometry and spectroscopy, combined with the analysis of its progenitor, explosion physics, and metallicity, provide valuable insights that contribute to the understanding of Type II supernovae with a short plateau duration. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. The proposed MuLE concept can also be applied to other types of optics, such as micro-channel plate (MCP) X-ray optics. The MuLE arrangement outperforms a single LE mirror centered on the image sensor in various aspects, offering a promising future for its application in various X-ray monitoring scenarios. To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. Ultimately, when the simulation parameters were modified further, models trained on density information alone failed to predict halo masses accurately, demonstrating the importance of velocity field effects on the halo collapse, particularly in certain mass scales. Lastly, when analyzing the influence of velocity field on halo formation, it was discovered that velocity information primarily affects the distribution of subhalos within larger halos. Lastly, an analytical model was used to replicate the findings of enhanced halo destruction within the regime of closed shells, aligning with the predicted effects of velocity field perturbations.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. 

These models have been compared to established theories and the effects of different parameter variations on the physics observed have been analyzed. This new formulation has been applied to the study of rotating stars with combinations of cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion processes, and has yielded accurate numerical results for a range of parameters. This method has significant implications for the study of rotating stars and it has the potential to tackle a wide range of physical problems in the field.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, our findings indicate that this method can be applied in conjunction with existing labeling methods, such as human validation, to produce high-quality results. Our proposed approach and accompanying code are available online at the following location: https://github.com/google/selective-labeling. Our research has the potential to act as a foundation for developing more scalable documentation analysis systems capable of handling visually complex documents. Our proposed approach can be applied in a wide range of applications, including but not limited to text-based validation systems, human-computer interaction interfaces, and annotation tools for machine learning models. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We detail a deep learning platform developed in-house, comprising tools for data management, network training, and visualization. This platform's potential applications extend beyond this specific analysis, making it suitable for tackling similar challenges in other areas of multi-messenger astronomy. We also demonstrate the advantages of using real LIGO data, finding that signals pre-wholved through Wiener filtering are more difficult to classify than directly analyzed signals. Lastly, we explore two potential approaches for enhancing detection efficiency in future installations. The previously developed network's limited memory prevents it from being applied to future detectors like the upgraded LIGO. We introduce a second network designed specifically for the upgraded LIGO, which showcases a significant improvement in detection efficiency when compared to the original network. This second network's structure is a combination of convolutional and recurrent layers, enabling it to handle longer signals and detect signals pre-wholved through Wiener filtering. We anticipate this double-layer network will be highly effective for future detectors like the upgraded LIGO and the proposed 2.5 GHz LIGO. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. Moreover, this study highlights the significance of studying contextual behavioral changes and reversible policies' lasting social effects in large-scale analyses. Finally, it provides a framework for assessing the long-term impact of temporary interventions on complex dynamic systems. The underlying dataset involves geospatial user category diversity metrics, aggregated at zip code levels in four major US cities, covering a 15-month period ending in late 2021. The code and underlying data are available at https://github.com/panapotis/.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in significant accretion bursts on its own. Rather, only the impact of high-density objects crossing a critical boundary can produce the observed effects. Key factors affecting accretion bursts include: the behavior of turbulent discs where objects can get stuck, as well as discs powered by magnetic winds that allow for bursts akin to those observed. Furthermore, interactions with thermal instabilities in the inner disk can influence the duration and intensity of bursts, while dense stars or migrating objects can produce different effects, such as mergers rather than bursts, and object disruptions that could result in super-Eddington outflows affecting their surroundings. Finally, in models depicting dense objects as low-mass protostars, the relationships between their mass, the mass of their stellar body, and the surrounding matter could all impact accretion and mergers, leading to diverse scenarios that could potentially reconcile observations of young stellar objects. Despite the importance of three-dimensional dynamics in forming dense objects, their subsequent interactions can often be predicted using one-dimensional models, especially when objects become trapped within the inner disk. However, the return to three-dimensional simulations is necessary to fully capture the diverse range of possible outcomes, including objects being ejected from the system or broken down into gas and stars. In response to the limited lifetime of high-mass stars, researchers have proposed various models involving massive stars formed from rapid accretion, but these need to account for the time it takes for high-mass protostars to form and reach their death. By simulating a range of scenarios and comparing them to observational evidence, the team behind this research found that: the lifetime of high-mass stars is typically 400,000 years, with a range of 300,000 to 600,000 years, and the majority of their mass is acquired during the final 50,000 years, with a range of 20,000 to 100,000 years. Additionally, the probability of a star being formed through the merger of two objects rather than accreting all its mass alone is approximately 30%. This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model against both direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and a comparable Dysthe equation proposed by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch, discovering that it accurately replicates their results across various levels of vorticity. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. Further testing on a larger campus with multiple layers, using up to five sonar sensors in real-time 3D navigation, is also documented. The proposed method is suitable for wide-range applications in indoor and semi-indoor environments. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/Abdullah-Al-Shikhah/NavController.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings highlight potential areas for improvement in the underlying architecture, specifically the limitations of large pre-trained language models like BERT, as well as opportunities for further innovation in the field of fake news detection. The code is available at: https://github.com/AhmedHamdy1991/CMTR-BERT.

In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture weights. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary. All finite admixture models can be viewed as special cases of this directed version, which is demonstrated by suitable transformations in the original and directed versions. A simulation study and an analysis of real data are used to evaluate the proposed algorithm's performance. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  We openly provide the DynaSOAr framework under an permissive BSD license to facilitate easy adoption across a range of object-oriented GPU applications.  Our framework source code is available at https://github.com/CompilersGroup/DynaSOAr.  We also include a brief DynaSOAr DSL language reference at the end of this document.  In addition to DynaSOAr, our research includes a theoretical framework for evaluating the efficiency of object-oriented programming on SIMD devices, which provides a set of guidelines and best practices for parallelizing object-oriented applications on these devices.  Finally, our results show that DynaSOAr's performance can be further enhanced by optimizing object layout, memory access, and method execution, which could be achieved by combining DynaSOAr with other GPU optimization tools and frameworks.  As such, DynaSOAr's efficient memory allocator can be used in conjunction with other GPU performance tuning tools to further speedup its application code, which is reflected in our benchmark results.  We believe that DynaSOAr's approach and results provide valuable insights and performance gains for a wide range of SMMO GPU applications. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state. This theoretical model highlights the complex interplay between spin-orbit coupling, superconducting energy gap, and magnetic interaction in a real system. Moreover, it emphasizes the necessity of precise analysis of local states, as well as the limited applicability of simplified models to magnetic impurity systems. Lastly, this framework facilitates prediction of unique low-energy phenomena for a wide range of magnetic and chemical perturbations.

In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, and further research into TOI-712, with a brightness of $9.9$, is worthwhile due to its relatively young and temperate conditions. Although follow-up spectroscopy showed that TOI-712 is a single star, the team couldn't rule out the possibility of additional planets or interactions with external bodies. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Lastly, our findings also highlight the necessity for accurate supercell sizing in order to obtain reliable results, as an under-sized supercell led to errors including anti-ferromagnetic ordering and N-O bonding.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. Lastly, this approach also measures the total cross-section for single top-quark production in the semi-elastic process. The analytical prediction for this cross-section at run II is approximately 12 picobarns. The elastic and semi-elastic cross-sections for run II are estimated to be 0.38 picobarns and 12 picobarns, respectively. The detection of the semi-elastic process at a efficiency of 30% is achievable with 3 inverse picobarns of data, whereas detecting the semi-elastic process at the same efficiency with a 30% uncertainty in the cross-section requires at least 10 inverse picobarns of data. The optimal acceptance window for detecting the semi-elastic process optimally is found to be $\ 4.5 < \eta_{\rm min} < 8.5$ and $\eta_{\rm max} = 8.5$ for runs with luminosity thresholds of $10^{31}$, $10^{32}$, and $10^{33}$ inverse centibarns, respectively. The analysis presented herein has been incorporated into the RooT framework as a new production of elastic top-quark processes in the TopCatalyst package. The predictions for the semi-elastic cross-section at run II are also in alignment with other calculations using MadGraph/MadEvent and the ATLAS elastic top-quark pair production code. In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Additionally, we demonstrate that both of these latter records are achieved with techniques that enable a more general result involving a specific graph combination. Lastly, our work also touches upon a related problem of determining the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the infinite binary tree, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. The record for this case, specifically for structures like cliques and odd cycles, is set at $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ and was previously unknown. The approach used here differs significantly from the method employed by Erdos and Spiga et al. and could be seen as a way to relate to their result. The most basic case involving a tree also provides a new upper bound for an associated parameter called the Ramsey number, with numbers like 19 for structures like cliques and odd cycles. Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits. To achieve over 90 percent accuracy, our estimates suggest that qutrits would require an order of magnitude more time (10^3 to 10^4 times) compared to qubits. To facilitate this research, we developed Python code incorporating the qudit amplitude damping and Pauli error channels into the NumPy and QuTip libraries. Our calculations also incorporate a proposal by Hamilton et al. to utilize thomson scattering to achieve qudit quantum error correction, though this prediction remains speculative. Our findings suggest that in the context of qudit QED simulations, developing better noise reduction methods or implementing quantum error correction protocols will be crucial for extending to larger dimensional qudits. Our code is available at https://github.com/AlexanderCruzan/sQED-noise-error.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, emitted with an enormous intensity of ten to the power of 12 per unit steradian. The degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted particles and their corresponding energies. In particular, the polarization is maximized at certain angles and reaches levels as high as sixty percent, primarily due to the unique interaction between the positrons and the intense laser fields within the overdense plasma. The occurrence of positron polarization is relatively robust, thereby likely manifesting in experiments using high-power lasers interacting with dense targets, with potential for a wide range of applications. The theoretical understanding of this phenomenon is also validated through the analysis of simulated spectra, with the predicted effects awaiting direct observation in ongoing and future experiments. The expected positivity of the results indicates that, with high-power lasers interacting with dense targets, there are vast opportunities for discovering new physics and expanding their uses in various fields. The proposed approach can be implemented in various settings, with the initial simulation conducted using a 50 micrometer thick target, although the effects are largely insensitive to the target's density. The proposed research can be further developed to optimize target designs, as well as the parameters of the laser and the electronic and positron states, with the potential outcomes awaiting direct observation in experiments. The theoretical understanding behind the results can be applied to validate the effects on the produced positrons and electrons through the analysis of simulated spectra, with the potential outcomes awaiting direct observation in experiments. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Furthermore, it demonstrates that groups with a diameter of the order n^k include those with a single conjugacy class, multiple orders of size, and a maximal solvable subgroup with a degree of k in its length. This leads to a group with a diameter of the order n^k for almost all element sizes, providing a concrete example of how the diameter changes as the group's structure changes. This research was influenced by a prior result attributed to Tointon. The proposed project also offers an alternative proof of a prior fact cited as Tointon's Result 1.23. The research presented here initially appeared as the author's PhD thesis. The main contribution of this research has been incorporated into a broader theorem by Tointon, which was published in a more recent paper, leaving this result specialized. Despite this development, the research presented here will be retained in its current form due to the significantly different approach used to achieve the same result, as well as the novel connection established with the project of developing a scalable diameter tester. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. The temperature sensor was further evaluated in a complex system that employs adaptive voltage and frequency scaling, resulting in a 12{\deg}C thermal design power reduction with the same system area. The proposed temperature sensor has been patented as part of the US Patent Number 20230104193. The design files for the proposed temperature sensor have been made available online at \url{https://github.com/temperature-sensor}. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  Such investigation will be crucial in clarifying the degree to which the core mass function influences the resulting star formation's mass.  Such an understanding is critical to better defining the factors that determine the massive star formation rate within molecular clouds.  On top of that, it also raises the question of whether massive star formation can originate from cores with masses similar to those observed in molecular cloud surveys.  Sufficient progress in this area will require fully mapping the mass distributions of both prestellar and protostellar cores across a broad range of environments.  In the context of the Dragon infrared dark cloud, we observe a distinct group of dense cores that fail to show associated outflow emission, suggesting they may represent an early stage of core formation, rather than a dormant stage.  These cores are compared to their outflow-associated counterparts, showing they possess similar mass distributions, but with different mass ratio distributions.  Ultimately, this research proves the concept that core mass growth is a widespread phenomenon, and it offers a potential path for forming massive stars, with the associated implications for the underlying physics that govern cloud evolution, the formation of both stellar masses and outflows, and the core mass function's impact on the resulting star formation's mass distribution. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. The resulting operator's effects are then expressed in the conventional expansion form. The process is illustrated by applying these operators to the fundamental zonal function, yielding new, uniformly convergent series representations. The paper also explores the connection between these operators and conventional methods, providing a means of transitioning between them. The introduced operators have inherent statistical interpretations, making them applicable in time-series analysis within the sphere domain. The paper concludes by demonstrating these operators' applications in such a sphere domain time-series analysis setting. The process involves constructing a set of discrete, uniformly convergent series representations of the spherical Laplace operator when applied to a given data set, allowing for the subsequent application of its positive definite properties. The resulting discussion centers on the choice of modeling spaces, with the paper proposing the use of non-strictly positive definite functions to enhance model flexibility without sacrificing statistical consistency. The proposed approach is then expressed in a compact form that can be directly applied to numerical analysis.
