The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. This relationship enables accurate prediction of the transition between these regimes, completing our understanding of the stick-slip to stationary transition in dry liquid foams. The findings of our study are relevant to various situations involving fluid dynamics, including the flow of liquids within porous media, emulsions, and foams, as well as the operation of devices like bubble columns and froth flotation equipment. The importance of surface roughness on fluid flow has also been illustrated in the accompanying figure. The roughness of surfaces can vary significantly, as shown in figures S1 to S3, which show examples of surface roughness observed in the laboratory and naturally occurring environments. The figure S4 depicts the stress-pattern diagram that can be achieved through stress measurements and visual observations, which is relevant to the study of complex systems involving dry liquid foams, bubble columns, and froth flotation equipment. The transition from the stick-slip to the stationary regime can be initiated by increasing the surface tension, as shown in the figure S6, changing the distribution of gas bubbles, as shown in the figure S7, changing the flow rate, as shown in the figure S8, or altering the surface roughness, as shown in the figure S9. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. The data and code used in this report are available at https://github.com/alexfawzi/iscnn.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes with both circumferentially confined folds and branches that occur with variations in the rate of rotation and imposed pressure. Bifurcation diagrams representing a variety of states, including both reflection-symmetric states and asymmetric states, are presented in this study. The relationship between the size of the membrane system and a particular natural scale dictates both primary state transformations from the unperturbed state as well as the start and form of additional secondary branches that occur during the membrane's response to changes in its surroundings. The study on a very elastic membrane provides a combination of both linear and nonlinear analysis that serves as a step towards understanding more complex situations, such as those involving fluid-filled cavities or multiple interacting membrane segments. The study on an inextensible membrane, on the other hand, offers a contrast by exhibiting similar behavior to a recent study on a specific type of elastic shell. The research also examines unique phenomena that occur in rotating systems, making it relevant to a wide range of fields beyond just the basic physics that it is based on. The occurrence of both large-amplitude, short-wavelength folds as well as a different type of instability that involves the formation of both branches and loops, makes this study particularly valuable. The research described in this paper is also part of a larger project that aims to explore more complex, three-dimensional situations in rotating systems. The development of an appropriate dimensionality reduction technique, as well as a new form of state variable that eliminates the distortion caused by the membrane's inextensibility, are key components of this project. The technique of reducing dimensionality has provided accurate results that match the results obtained from three-dimensional simulations in a variety of different situations, making it a highly effective method. The new state variable has not only eliminated the membrane's distortion but has also revealed the relationship between the membrane's natural scale and different state transitions, as well as other important phenomena. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/ghrua/look-ahead-attention.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science. By studying the past of grid computing, we aim to provide a useful example for the field of artificial intelligence. Just as grid computing provides a foundation to build upon, artificial intelligence can build upon the foundations of grid computing. We also explore the relationship between grid computing and artificial intelligence, noting that artificial intelligence represents a more comprehensive and richer field of study that includes grid computing as a subset. In the process, we offer guidance on how to define the boundaries of artificial intelligence and highlight the benefits of doing so. Ultimately, our discussion highlights the value of adopting a translational perspective when exploring the development of complex technologies and the importance of differentiating between multiple layers of abstraction that make up these technologies. We conclude by providing a future-oriented analysis of the relationship between grid computing and artificial intelligence. We propose a variety of research directions that aim to integrate the strengths of grid computing with the richness of artificial intelligence. In the process, we offer a potential definition of artificial intelligence that includes grid computing as a subset and provides a framework for evaluating research in artificial intelligence. In the process, we explore the relationship between grid computing and artificial intelligence from a historical perspective, noting that artificial intelligence represents a continuous evolution of ideas and technologies that originated in the 1950s. We conclude by providing a future-oriented analysis of the relationship between grid computing and artificial intelligence, noting that artificial intelligence will continue to evolve and change, and that grid computing provides a foundation to build upon. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. This achievement extends the available operating range of the source, and allows it to produce plasma in the helicon mode even with imperfect antenna design. A better understanding of the source was gained, and it is now available for a variety of experiments, including investigating wave absorption, studying how plasma interacts with waves in the helicon mode, and testing components for full-size plasma devices. Furthermore, this source can be used to study plasma in conditions similar to those found in ASDEX upgrade, one of the leading experimental tokamaks, and provides a foundation for a next-generation plasma source that could be used in devices like the W7-X stellarator. This knowledge can also be applied to other sources with similar designs, and it is valuable for creating new sources that can operate in the helicon mode. This achievement is particularly significant because it shows that it is possible to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode using a single-loop antenna, which was previously thought to be impossible. This development will likely be useful for a wide range of plasma applications, including but not limited to ICRF plasma sources. This work was presented at the 33rd IEEE Symposium on Plasma Science and Technology and the 23rd Topical Conference on Radio Frequency Power in Plasma Heating and Current Drive.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Moreover, this methodology enables researchers to demonstrate the significance of model performance for binary mask prediction alone, rather than on density mask prediction alone. Experimental evaluations conducted on three separate datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with the W-Net model achieving superior performance compared to standard U-Net, LinkNet, and FPN models. Moreover, this approach has been applied to analyze lymph node images, with the resulting masks revealing notable structural features that correspond to specific lymph node structures. The complexity of this model, the W-Net, is further simplified to a basic U-Net in the subsequent analysis, with the resulting output masks from this simplified model revealing similar structural features present in the original images. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/ghruan/W-Net. The datasets used in this research are available online at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/?vgbmkz1z4g, https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/?vgbmkz1z4g, and https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/?vgbmkz1z4g. The research presented in this paper was conducted in partnership with the Department of Pathology, Chang Gung Memorial Hospital. The authors declare no conflicts of interest in this research project.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Specifically, the results indicate a 13 dB boost in the signal-to-noise ratio of lateral displacement estimation in simulations and a 5 dB gain in experimental settings. Moreover, the findings demonstrate OVERWIND's robustness against the choice of regularization parameters. In conclusion, the integration of VSSA with OVERWIND ELASTOGRAPHY yields a landmark achievement in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Hence, this study presents VSSA BEAMFORMING, VSSA OVERWIND, and the proposed technique as a platform for elastography research. This approach has vast potential for development and can be applied to other elastography techniques. Finally, the technique's potential is demonstrated by imaging soft tissue with embedded objects, and it outperforms SA OVERWIND in terms of signal-to-noise ratio. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Moreover, by incorporating a learning element, our model exhibits potential in dynamic and uncertain environments. We illustrate the versatility of our hierarchical model by integrating it with a range of individual games, including those with uncertain maps, time-varying grids, and tree-like structures. Our work offers a platform for further incorporation of external data, dynamic models, and machine learning techniques to enhance the performance of hierarchical pursuit-evasion games. Our code is available at https://github.com/Zongwei-WEI/Hierarchical-Pursuit-Evasion.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our research highlights the challenges and opportunities in multi-task
reinforcement learning settings and showcases a straightforward yet effective way
to exploit task sharing, namely by employing modular dynamics models. Lastly, we
analytically and numerically analyze the phenomenon of performance degradation
caused by task sharing, providing insights that can guide future research. Our code
is available at https://github.com/ghul131/multitask-dynamics-networks.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. By transforming the proposed function u, we are able to establish a relationship with the original conditions of the Riemann-Hilbert problem. This relationship enables the transformation of the three balls theorem to be formulated in terms of the original variables. As a result, this formulation allows us to extend the three balls theorem to the space R^n+1, and consequently to the hyperbolic space H^n+1. Furthermore, this extension is demonstrated to be equivalent to the original problem through the Baer-Souček transform. This paper also introduces a new approach to proving the Bompastor-Caruana theorem, which is a two circles theorem. Additionally, this paper provides a comprehensive discussion on the application of the three balls theorem to the eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator in the space R^n+1. This discussion involves the derivation of a non-trivial estimate for the norm of the eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator in the space R^n+1. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. By incorporating noise as input to the conditional GAN, we significantly enhanced the quality of sampled images. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/shoukaiwang/CGAN-posterior-sampling.

We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Furthermore, calculations determine the distance to this screen as well as the extent and characteristics of the void, contributing to the mapping of the Local Bubble's structure. Additionally, the analysis reveals a screen that exhibits a decade-timescale variation in scintillation patterns, likely caused by the screen's movement or the change in void size. The data also reveal a dispersed screen that shows a distribution of scattering lengths in the line of sight to the pulsar, without any detectable void or gas associated with it. The findings from this paper are consistent with previous research suggesting that the distribution of scattering lengths in the line of sight to the pulsar is directly related to the three-dimensional structure of the interstellar medium. The three-dimensional structure was reconstructed using the scattering lengths and screen positions to create a comprehensive picture of the local interstellar medium around PSR B1133+16. The analysis of the data and the resulting reconstruction of the local interstellar medium around the pulsar B1133+16 provide a framework for interpreting similar data from future pulsar scintillation observations. The code used for the analysis has been made available for public access. The reconstruction of the local interstellar medium around PSR B11316 can be visualized in a three-dimensional model available for interactive exploration. The discovery of a screen associated with a decade-timescale variation in scintillation patterns remains unprecedented and requires further investigation to determine the cause of the change. The distribution of scattering lengths in the line of sight to the pulsar is unique and provides a new insight into the structure of the local interstellar medium, offering a framework for analyzing similar distributions in the lines of sight to other pulsars. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Code is available at: https://github.com/Parandkuhi/Quasi-Periodic_WaveNet.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/zhoukui, along with the VGG-Sound Source dataset accessible at https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/data/vggsound_source.html.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. LGCN's simplicity and efficiency make it suitable for a wide range of applications, from recommender systems to molecular graph representations. The code for LGCN is available at https://github.com/JinHePro/LGCN.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. This inverse problem is ill-posed, and therefore, we develop a quasi-optimality cost functional to convert it into a well-posed problem. This functional aims to minimize the error between the proposed solution and the exact source, restricted by the structural acoustic PDE model and certain regularity constraints. We establish the differentiability class of the operator defining this cost functional, which in turn yields the differentiability class of the solution to the inverse problem. Finally, we implement a gradient-based algorithm to solve the inverse problem and provide numerical results to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. This study was motivated by a real-world application involving the identification of sources of noise within an aircraft wing using optical methods. Although the mathematical model can be optical-based, the algorithm developed here is suitable for any measurement method. The research was conducted in collaboration with the aerospace industry and optical experts, and involved developing a statistical framework to validate the solution and the algorithm, which can be extended to other optical-based inversion problems. The numerical code developed as part of this research can be accessed through the website http://cag.diku.dk/. We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, we establish that our model's impulse control
equation aligns with the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting model, offering a more
advanced analysis of this relationship. Our model's impulse control equation
also enables us to determine the optimal discount parameter for minimizing
impulsivity, which we find to be $1-\rho$, where $\rho$ is the impulse control
threshold. Lastly, we establish that our model's impulse control equation can be
interpreted through the lens of the Nudge Theory, particularly in addressing
issues of food waste and obesity. We support these claims with numerical
experiments. Our model's and the Tsallis delay discounting model's impulse control
equations differ, with the Tsallis model's equation implying that the optimal
discount parameter is $1/\rho$, where $\rho$ is the impulse control threshold.
This conclusion is also supported by the data, with both models yielding similar
results for low levels of impulsivity. We find that the optimal impulse control
threshold $\rho$ depends on the degree of impulsivity and delay period. For a
given delay period, the impulse control threshold $\rho$ increases with the
degree of impulsivity, indicating that a more diverse population requires a
higher $\rho$ value to minimize impulsivity. On the other hand, for a degree of
impulsivity equal to 4, the impulse control threshold $\rho$ decreases with the
delay period. We also find that the exponential delay discounting model
overestimates the impulse cost compared to our model, which is reflected in the
exponential model's higher $\rho$ value. This result implies that the
exponential delay discounting model is less sensitive to changes in the delay
period. Finally, we demonstrate that our model's and the Tsallis delay discounting model's impulse costs differ, with the Tsallis model's impulse cost increasing more rapidly than our model's, which is supported by the data. graphical interface that simplifies data import, methodology selection, and
visualization customization. ViDaExpert is a platform-independent application

was supported by the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS). The

The application includes a module for creating interactive web-based 3D visualizations that can be accessed from the website. The development of ViDaExpert aimed to create an open framework for nonlinear visualization and analysis of complex data and has been registered as free software. The application enables direct data import from popular spreadsheet software such as Excel, in addition to support for various 3D models and mesh files, including STL, OBJ, and PLY. The development of ViDaExpert was influenced by the requirements of various projects and research, including the analysis of artifacts and historical objects. The application includes a module for automatic generation of realistic material properties for 3D models, enabling the creation of highly realistic 3D scenes from data, in addition to support for texture mapping
